title: Ashes
logline: Ash Wednesday in Mid-City and the long way home: ashes from the man who poured the water, a porch full of Broussards with questions that go unanswered, thirty-five hours in a van where nobody touches anybody, a pack he doesn’t open — and on Saturday, a priest who used to be a doctor.

s01.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:20 AM · N. DUPRE STREET, THE ATTIC
body: It’s barely light, and what light there is comes in gray at the gable window, through the blades of a box fan that hasn’t turned since summer. Over Jack’s face the points of the roofing nails stand through the deck boards, each with a bead of the night’s cold on it. Remy’s Tiger poster has let go of its second corner and hangs by one tack now, Tiger upside down with his fist still up, still celebrating. The hangover sits behind Jack’s eyes like the heel of a hand pressing in. Up through the open hatch from the front room comes Mémère’s television with the sound kept low for the sleepers: EWTN, the Ash Wednesday Mass from somewhere in Alabama, a choir singing something slow he can’t make out a word of.

They got home from the Quarter a little after half past twelve, and at one Clovis was still out on the porch swing in his good jacket with a bottle of Old Forester on the boards by his shoe and a Kool going. He has smoked his Kools on that porch since 1989, the year Tony quit cigarettes on a paper sack of sunflower seeds in his shirt pocket and put Clovis and his Kools out the front door. Remy sat on the top step in the purple wig, and Theo on the step below him, and Clovis poured for the three of them into jelly glasses with the cartoons washed off. Jack took a finger of it, and then another, because his hands needed to be holding something that wasn’t a Marlboro; and when that didn’t work he went in and up the ladder in the dark and came back down with the January pack out of the side pocket of his duffel, eight left in it, and put it in Clovis’s shirt pocket behind the Kools. Clovis looked down at his own pocket. “That’s not how Lent works, cher.”

Up here, with the light coming, Jack can still hear his answer. “It’s how mine works.” Clovis buttoned the pocket down over them and poured him one more he didn’t drink, and that was all anybody said about it. Celeste was asleep. Lena had gone straight in from the car and shut the door of the girls’ room behind her.

He hasn’t lit one since the air pump in El Paso, twelve days ago. Whatever his body wanted out of them, it quit asking somewhere in Louisiana. His hands haven’t quit. Twice before he’s properly awake he catches them going to the breast pocket of the flannel he slept in, where there’s nothing, and then out to the Carhartt on its nail, to the pocket where the tin rode for two months, and that’s two different nothings. Forty days. The first morning of a thing knows exactly how long it is.

He gets onto his knees on the boards under the window, with his head going like a bass drum two blocks off, and gets through the penance from memory. Thirteen mornings now. The Twelve go out two by two with a walking stick and nothing else, no bread, no money in their belts, into the houses that will have them and the houses that won’t, and halfway through comes *shake the dust off your feet*, and he says it and goes on to the oil and the sick. When he stands, the attic tips and settles.

Kevin is dressed already, sitting by the hatch on his rolled-up sleeping bag in the windbreaker and a pair of khakis with a crease ironed into them somewhere between Marisol and here, his hair combed wet and straight back. He looks across the attic at Jack, and his nose makes a small, private, clinical decision.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says. “You smell like Clovis.”

body.text: He feels in the pocket of the windbreaker and takes something out and looks at it in his palm: the wax 7 off Monday’s cake, the wick gone black, the 7 a little bent from the heat. He puts it back and zips the pocket shut over it.

body: In the middle Theo is a long shape under the Marisol blanket, flat on his back, with his eyes open on the nails. He doesn’t turn his head.
“I’m coming to the ashes,” Theo says. “Don’t make it a thing.”
“It’s not a thing.”
“Good.”
From the foot of the ladder Celeste’s whisper comes up through the hatch, the one that carries the length of a ward without waking anybody in a bed: “Eight o’clock. Coffee’s not food.”

The RAZR is on the sill by his knee with its outside screen lit. One message, from Burnaby, sent at 6:14 by his clock, which is 4:14 by hers: the end of a night on the lot, the rain towers shut down, the trailers dark, and Skye in a doorway somewhere with her hood up and the night’s makeup still on.

s02.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:55 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — COFFEE IS NOT FOOD
body: There’s no breakfast. All week the kitchen has met him at the foot of the stairs with something going — grits, eggs, Monday’s red beans — and this morning the Magic Chef is cold on three burners, and on the fourth there’s the pot of chicory, and that is the menu. The 13-inch at the end of the counter is dark. The transistor that lives on top of the icebox went to Banks Street with Tony at five.

Celeste is home. She traded a girl in the ICU for Thursday, and she stands at the counter in a black cardigan setting out cups in a row, counting cups and not people. “Tony left at five,” she says. “Lent is Christmas for a fish market. He’ll meet us at church.”

Mémère has the head of the table, in black to the wrists, with a mantilla folded square in her lap and her beads going through her fingers. She has fasted every Ash Wednesday since before Truman, and she sits at an oilcloth with nothing on it but the sugar bowl as though the company were only late.
Josie, in her plaid uniform, has her book bag hung on the back of her chair, packed since six, and has done the reading. “The Church says you stop at fifty-nine, Mémère.”
Mémère answers her in French, at some length, without lifting her eyes off the beads.
“She says,” Josie reports, “fifty-nine is a number a man made up.”
Celeste lays down the law over the cups: the twins go at seven-twenty to Mass with their class and are home at two-thirty, and nobody in this family leaves this house for California till they are.

Remy is at the table’s elbow in last night’s sunglasses, gray under them, with both hands around an empty cup. “I’m giving up ‘brother-in-law’ for Lent,” he announces. “Forty days. After that, no promises.”
“That’s not a thing you can give up,” says Josie.
“It’s a *vice*, Josie.”

Laney has come down in a black dress from the waist down and a Pi Lam sweatshirt from the waist up, the biggest sunglasses in the parish, and Coco tucked under one arm like an evening clutch. She lays her cheek on the oilcloth, cool side down, and leaves it there. Margot sits across from her with a paperback Durkheim propped against the sugar bowl, pink and rested and turning pages, the only person in the house who slept. Kevin has his hands folded on the table. Theo has a cup of coffee in front of him that he doesn’t drink and doesn’t push away.
“Is aspirin food?” Laney asks, without lifting her cheek.
“Aspirin’s medicine, baby,” Celeste says, and sets two on a saucer by Laney’s ear, with a glass of water beside it, the way she’d set them on a tray at the foot of a bed.

body.text: On the counter by the bread box sits a Tupperware with a strip of masking tape across the lid and KEVIN on the tape in Celeste’s marker, and under the lid the last of Monday’s lemon pound cake. “For Thursday,” Celeste says, when she sees him see it. “Today you fast.” Kevin looks at the tape and keeps his hands folded, and then he looks out the window over the sink.

On the counter by the bread box sits a Tupperware with KEVIN across the lid in Laney’s silver Sharpie, a little crown drawn over the V, and under the lid the last of Monday’s lemon pound cake. “For Thursday,” Celeste says, when she sees him see it. “Today you fast.” Kevin looks at the crown and keeps his hands folded, and then he looks out the window over the sink.

body: Jack is at the stove end with his back to the counter when Lena comes down the stairs at seven, in a black dress with her jean jacket over it, the chest pocket buttoned down over the square of the tin, and a black lace mantilla in one hand. She goes past him to the stove and pours two coffees, his first, as she has every morning this week — the chicory, then the milk, without asking how — and she carries his the length of the oilcloth and sets it down at the far end, at the last place, in front of the chair by the back door. She takes hers up to the other end, beside Mémère, and sits down with the mantilla in her lap.
Laney lifts her cheek off the oilcloth to look at her. “Magdalena Broussard. You look like a widow in a Western.”
“It’s Ash Wednesday, cher.”
“I know what day it is.” The cheek goes back down. “I can *feel* what day it is.”
Yesterday on St. Charles, with half this family on the neutral ground to see it, she stood inside his coat through all of Rex. This morning there is the length of the table and a sugar bowl.
Josie has stopped halfway to the back door with one arm through a strap of her bag, and looks from one end of the table to the other.
“Did y’all have a fight?”
“No,” Lena says.
“Then why are you sitting like *that*?”
“It’s Lent.”
“Lent’s not about *chairs*.”
Mémère has been watching both ends of the oilcloth over her beads. She says something in French, short.
Josie translates. “She says it’s the first sensible thing she’s seen all week.”
At the counter Celeste puts the extra cups back in the cabinet one at a time, without looking at either end of the table. “Hm.”

choices.text: *Drink the coffee where she put it.*
response: He walks the length of the oilcloth to it and drinks it standing at the far end, by the back door, hot enough to hurt, with the hangover sitting on his eyes. Lena doesn’t look up from hers. Mémère gives one small nod over the beads, as at a hymn taken in the right key.
Celeste takes the car keys down off the nail, and that is the end of a breakfast that never started.
“It’s the *same* table,” says Josie.
Mémère laughs once, short and dry, over her beads. At her end Lena drinks her coffee like it’s evidence.
Celeste holds Josie’s coat open behind her, and Josie, still arguing, backs into it.
Josie narrows her eyes at him. “Then *what*.”
Lena answers from her end, in the voice that runs a fish-market counter on a Friday. “Then get your other strap, Josephine. It’s seven-twenty.”

Celeste has Jude’s collar straightened and both twins out the back door by the time the clock agrees with her, and then she turns around and looks at the rest of them, and at the coats on their hooks.

s03.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:00 AM · OUR LADY OF THE HOLY ROSARY, ESPLANADE AVENUE — DUST
body: They go up Esplanade to it on foot under the oaks, with last night’s beads still hanging in the branches, purple and green and gold gone dull in the gray; Celeste’s car creeps along at the curb beside them because Mémère will not be driven to her ashes, and Mémère walks on Remy’s arm, because this morning he needs hers more.

Inside the doors, at the back, there’s a holy water font on a pedestal, a marble shell with a chip out of the rim, and everybody going in touches it: Mémère, Remy, the women in scrubs, a man in a hard hat. Lena dips her fingers on her way past and crosses herself. Jack touches the water after her and does the same, and it’s cold, and it’s the same water.

Holy Rosary is fuller than any Sunday. It isn’t a holy day of obligation, and Esplanade Avenue has never cared: they are in the pews in work clothes and scrubs and one Saints jersey, standing two deep at the back under the loft. The church has gone purple overnight. The flowers are gone. On the altar there’s nothing but the cross, and on a small table at the foot of the steps a glass bowl of ash. A cantor up in the loft sings something alone, without the organ, a Lenten chant whose name Jack doesn’t know and whose shape he does.

The Broussards have their two pews on the Gospel side, Mémère on the aisle. The school has the first six rows, and the twins are in among their class in plaid and white. Halfway through the entrance chant Josie turns clear around in her pew to check on the family, and Jude reaches over and turns her back.

Tony comes in at the opening prayer, late from the market, in his green canvas jacket with ice melting off the cuffs and the case still on him, brine and cold steel, and kneels at the end of the pew beside Jack without taking it off. He prays the way he does, aloud, with his eyes open on the crucifix.
“Lord. It’s Lent. You know what that means for my business. Thank You.”
He crosses himself. Then, lower, like a man adding a line to an order: “And whatever it is with the boy. That one’s Yours.”

Theo is at the far end of the second pew, very still, with his hands between his knees. Laney has her sunglasses pushed up into her hair. Margot has her notebook shut in her lap, and when Laney looks over at her she says, “Participant observation,” which means she’s going up. Kevin kneels with his back straight and his eyes shut.

Jack’s hangover takes the readings one line at a time. From Joel, a lector in a navy suit: *rend your hearts, not your garments.* From Matthew, in Hébert’s dry little voice, *anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to be fasting,* and Jack has a thought about that one he doesn’t have the head to finish.

In between, the cantor sings the psalm alone and the church sings the refrain back to her, *Be merciful, O Lord, for we have sinned*, four hundred people and Tony, who sings it loudest and a half-step under everybody else, a man who has paid for the note and means to get it. Down the pew Jack can pick Lena’s voice out of all of it, low and sure, and he stops singing for a line to hear it, and then makes himself start again.
Hébert comes down to the foot of the altar steps for the homily, seventy-four years old and no taller than Josie, and keeps it short, in the voice from Breaux Bridge.

“Yesterday this whole city put on a mask. Today He puts a little dirt on your face so you can’t hide behind it — and then the Gospel tells you to go wash your face and not make a show. You will wear it out that door anyway. Wear it humble.”
He goes back up and sits down, and four hundred people who have known him for twenty-six years are surprised anyway.
*Wear it humble.* Jack has never worn anything humble in his life. He wears the Carhartt like he’s expecting to get into a fight in it.

Then the ashes. The family goes up in family order: Mémère first on Remy’s arm, Tony with the ice on his cuffs, Celeste. Hébert says something to Mémère in French that makes her lift her chin, and something to Tony that makes him snort in the middle of the aisle. At the end of the pew Celeste stops, takes Jack by the elbow without a word, moves him out of his place and into the one behind Lena, and goes on up the aisle ahead of them both.

So he goes up behind her, close enough in the line to see the back of her neck under the black lace: the clasp of the medal chain he fastened for her by her grandmother’s tomb, the mended link, a strand of hair the mantilla didn’t catch. He keeps his hands folded in front of him, the right one holding the left one down.

At the bowl Hébert looks up at her. He baptized her at the font by the side altar, nineteen years ago this summer; he poured the water. He puts his thumb in the ash and makes the cross on her forehead, a short stroke down and a short one across.
“Remember that you are dust, and to dust you will return.”
And then, lower, for her and for nobody else in the church: “Magdalena.”
“Amen,” she says, and steps aside.

Then it’s Jack. The same words he’s heard every Ash Wednesday of his life at St. Brigid’s, in that other voice, and the thumb, cold and gritty, pressing a little harder than it has to, as if to make sure it takes. Hébert looks at him over the bowl.
“*Le garçon de l’Ohio.*”

On the way back down the side aisle a crumb of the ash comes loose and catches in his lashes, and he carries it to the pew at the bottom edge of everything he looks at, a small gray blur he doesn’t brush away.

Behind him the rest of them go up. Margot takes hers with her chin raised, a specimen offering itself to the slide. Laney shuts her eyes for it and holds Coco against her hip. Kevin bows his head so low that Hébert has to reach. Theo takes his without a word and goes back to the end of the second pew, and the ash on him is very black.

Kneeling, with dirt on his face and the hangover behind it, he has to decide what it’s for. *Remember that you are dust.* He knows dust. In Youngstown it came down out of the stacks along the river onto every car on Glenwood Avenue for seventy years, the old men at St. Brigid’s say, and the morning it quit coming down was worse. On Royal Street he told Skye you give it to Somebody; it’s a present; the going without is the wrapping paper. Forty days of wrapping paper. Now he has to choose what goes inside.

body.text: At midnight under a streetlight on Esplanade he told her he’d say one for her in the morning, and he says it first, before anything else: a Hail Mary all the way through, for a girl asleep in a trailer in Burnaby.

body: Two places down the pew Lena kneels upright with her folded hands against her mouth, and from where he is he can see her in profile under the lace: the gray cross on her forehead, a grain of it fallen onto the bridge of her nose, her eyes shut. Nine hours ago he could feel her shivering through his shirt. He looks at the altar instead, at the bare cross and the bowl, and keeps looking at it, and the not-looking is work he has to do with every muscle in his neck.
At the far end of the pew Theo kneels with his eyes open.

choices.text: *Offer it for Skye — that Tuesday doesn’t break her.*
choices.key: At Holy Rosary on Ash Wednesday you offered your Lent for Skye — that Tuesday wouldn’t break her.
response: He thinks of her asleep in a trailer on the lot in Burnaby with the white phone on the pillow by her face, and he gives Him the whole forty days for one evening on Del Playa: that she comes out the other side of it on her feet. It’s the first prayer he has ever said for her that he can’t tell her about.

choices.text: *Offer it for the truth — that you tell it right, every word, to her face.*
choices.key: At Holy Rosary on Ash Wednesday you offered your Lent for the truth — that you’d tell it right, every word, to her face.
response: Not for how it comes out. For the words: that on Tuesday they come in the right order, every one of them true, and not one of them a kindness that’s really a lie. He asks for that with his forehead on his knuckles, harder than he’s asked for anything since Christmas.

choices.text: *Offer it for Lena on Sunday, and for Julian.*
choices.key: At Holy Rosary on Ash Wednesday you offered your Lent for Lena on Sunday, and for Julian.
response: For the two of them at a table somewhere after Mass on Sunday, and for the kind man who is going to be kind about it. He finds it’s harder to pray for Julian than for anybody he knows, and he does it anyway, twice, until the second time it takes.

choices.text: *Offer it the way you always do — for your brother.*
choices.key: At Holy Rosary on Ash Wednesday you offered your Lent for your brother, the way you always do.
response: Danny, in a cell in Leavittsburg, where there are no ashes this morning unless a deacon carries some in. It’s what Jack has offered every Lent since Danny went in, and he offers it again now, all forty days of it, toward a debt to his brother that forty days won’t touch.

s04.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:05 AM · THE STEPS OF HOLY ROSARY, ESPLANADE AVENUE — CROOKED
body: At the sign of peace he shakes Tony’s cold hand and Celeste’s warm one, and past her mother Lena gives him a nod, a small one, and he gives her one back. He goes up for Communion behind her, because that’s still the order they’re in, and then it’s the dismissal with no hymn after it, and the doors at the back swing open on Esplanade and the cold comes in to meet the crowd.

Outside, the avenue is gray and wet under the oaks, the beads still up in the branches. Everybody on it has the smudge. The driver of the Esplanade bus has one, pulling away from the stop with both hands on the wheel. A woman pushing a stroller has one, and so does the baby. Two cops in a cruiser at the light have one each. It’s like coming out into a city where everybody has been told the same thing about themselves and has decided to wear it to work.

Laney has the six of them in a row on the steps before the crowd thins, and hands her pink BlackBerry to Remy, who takes the picture from two steps down in his sunglasses, sideways and then the other way. Lena is on one end of the row and Jack on the other. Theo stands next to Laney with his ashes very black and his face doing nothing; Margot has her arms crossed; Kevin stands up straight, like a groomsman.
“Six sinners and a coconut,” Laney says, and holds Coco up beside her face for it.
“Everybody say *dust*,” Remy says from behind the phone, and nobody does, and he takes it anyway.
The phone makes its little shutter noise. At the curb Tony is back in his truck already, the engine going, and Celeste has Mémère by the elbow, walking her down to the car.

Then the row breaks up and the others go down the steps, and Jack and Lena are left at the top of them, a little apart, with the doors open behind them and people coming out around them on both sides. It’s the first time they’ve been alone in daylight since the levee, if this is alone.

Down at the bottom of the steps a man in a Sewerage & Water Board jacket stops with his ashes on to light a cigarette, cupping it out of the wind, and the smell of it comes up the steps on the damp. Jack’s hands go into the pockets of the Carhartt and make fists there. Lena’s eyes go to his pockets and come back up to his face.
She looks at his forehead.
“It’s crooked.”
“Hébert’s eighty.”
“He’s seventy-four. It’s crooked.”

Her hand comes up. It’s her thumb, out toward the smudge to put it right, the way you’d fix a child’s collar at the school door, and it stops an inch from his forehead. It holds there. He can feel it without feeling it, the cold of her hand on the air against his skin, and every part of him that has been told no since midnight goes and stands at that inch. He doesn’t lean. Her hand goes down into her jacket instead, flat on the buttoned flap of the chest pocket, over the tin.
In the breast pocket of the Carhartt the RAZR goes off. His father.

body: He answers the same way, one key at a time, with the cracked hinge creaking and Lena watching him type it.

body.text: 8 AM. HOLY ROSARY. CROOKED.
GOOD.

body: From Frank Costigan, in capitals, that is a parade. Jack shuts the phone.
“You answered him in kind,” Lena says.
“It’s the only language he reads.”
“Mama’s going to ask me in the car,” Lena says.
“What are you going to tell her?”
“‘Lent, Mama.’ And she’s going to say ‘Hm.’”

Down at the curb her mother is settling Mémère into the front seat with a hand on the top of her head to mind the door frame, and Lena watches that, and then she doesn’t. “I’m not going to be able to look at you till Tuesday.”

She says it looking straight at him, the ash on her a little smeared at one arm of the cross where the lace caught it, and her eyes are the one thing on Esplanade Avenue that isn’t gray. He holds them as long as she does.

choices.key: On the steps of Holy Rosary Lena said your ashes were crooked and nearly fixed them. You told her to leave them.
response: She takes her hand off the pocket and doesn’t use it for anything.
“…Leave it,” she agrees, and looks at the cross on his forehead as if she’s memorizing which way it leans.

choices.text: “Matthew six. You’re supposed to wash your face.”
response: “Matthew six is about showing *off*, Youngstown. You’ve never shown off a day in your life.”
That came out nearly kind. She corrects it. “It’s still crooked.”

choices.key: On the steps of Holy Rosary Lena said she couldn’t look at you till Tuesday. You told her you couldn’t look at her either.
response: “Then we’re both going to be very interested in Texas.”
She looks down Esplanade instead, hard, at the oaks and the bus and the beads, like it’s all going to be on a test.

s04a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:15 AM · ESPLANADE AVENUE, AT THE CURB
body: Lena goes down the steps ahead of him to her mother’s car and gets into the back seat behind Mémère, to go home and pack, and pulls the door shut. The rest of them are already strung out up Esplanade on foot toward Dupre under the oaks, Remy out in front, Laney carrying Coco in both arms, Margot with her collar up. Jack stands on the bottom step with the ash on his face and his hands still in his pockets.
At the same second, at the curb behind the car, Tony leans across the cab of his truck with the passenger window down and the market still on him.

body.text: “Ohio. I could use a man who knows ice.”
body.else: “Ohio. I could use a man who can lift.”

body: And Celeste, at her own door with the keys in her hand, across the roof of the car: “Baby, Mémère wants you at the house.”

They hear each other. Tony keeps his arm along the back of the seat. Celeste keeps her hand on the door. In the front seat, through the glass, with her mantilla off and folded on her knee, Mémère lifts two fingers at Jack and crooks them: come.

response: Tony has the door open before Jack is off the curb. Celeste gets in behind the wheel and pulls her own door shut.

He gets into the back of Celeste’s car with Mémère’s mantilla handed back and laid on the seat between him and Lena’s elbow, and out at the curb Tony slaps the side of the truck twice, like a horse he’s fond of, and pulls out into Esplanade.

s05h.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:40 AM → 1:30 PM · DUPRE STREET — THE DAYBED
s05h.music: Mahalia Jackson — “Move On Up a Little Higher”
body: At twenty to ten Celeste is building a cooler on the oilcloth the way she would stock a crash cart: everything in reach, nothing where it doesn’t belong, and nothing touched that she hasn’t handed over. Jack has been handed the lid. He holds it.

Shrimp po’boys for tomorrow, the bread in one roll of butcher paper and the fried shrimp in another, because a po’boy dressed on Wednesday is a soggy disgrace by Thursday and she has standards even for Texas. A paper sack of Plaquemines satsumas, the leaves still on two of them. Pralines in wax paper. A thermos of coffee with THURSDAY on a strip of tape around its middle.
“Today you fast,” Celeste says. “That’s for tomorrow. If anybody opens that thermos in Louisiana, I’ll know.”

body.text: Last of all, a Tupperware with KEVIN on the lid in her own marker: what’s left of the lemon pound cake, wedged in at an angle so it rides flat.
Last of all, a Tupperware with KEVIN on the lid in Laney’s silver Sharpie, a crown drawn over the V: what’s left of the lemon pound cake, wedged in at an angle so it rides flat.

Then she takes the pie tin with the boysenberry ghost still in the corner down off the top of the refrigerator, washed and dried since the night they came, and opens Mémère’s cedar box on the sideboard, and fills the tin with pralines. One at a time. Each one in its own square of wax paper, laid in flat, edge to edge, the next row on top of the first.

body: Jack holds the lid and watches his debt to Gloria get paid off in sugar by a woman he met a week and a half ago.
“A tin goes back full, baby.” Celeste presses its lid on with the heel of her hand. “That’s not manners. That’s law.”

She tears a sheet of butcher paper off the roll, for the satsumas, and folds it, and with her eyes on the fold and her voice just above a whisper, she says, “I’ve been a nurse thirty years.” Another fold. “I know what a person looks like the morning after they’ve decided something.” She runs her thumbnail down the crease. “I don’t need to know what.” She takes the cooler lid out of his hands and puts it on and snaps both latches. “Do it right.”

She doesn’t wait to see what he’ll say, and he doesn’t say anything, and at ten o’clock she has the okra on the board and the onions going in the black pot for half past one, and the kitchen is a kitchen again.

Through the doorway, up the hall, he can see into the girls’ room: the end of the bed, and Lena’s bag open on it. She packs by sections, the way she argues. The black dress from this morning, folded in thirds. The jean jacket hung on the doorknob with its chest pocket buttoned down. She doesn’t come into the kitchen while he’s in it. He doesn’t go up the hall. Twice she crosses her own doorway with her arms full, and the second time he’s looking, and her back goes a little straighter going by.

The third time she stops in it to shake out the mantilla before she folds it, and holds it up to the window behind her by two corners, and the gray light comes through the lace onto her face. She hasn’t washed. The cross Hébert gave her is still on her forehead, a little crooked, the same as his. He stands in the kitchen with a roll of butcher paper in his hands and looks at it down the length of the hall, at that and at the dark place in the lace where her hair has been, and does not go to the doorway, and it costs what he knew it would, and he pays it.
At eleven Remy comes down the attic ladder in his sunglasses and lies on the linoleum in front of the stove because it’s warm there, and asks if a man can die of Lent.
“Not on the first day,” Celeste says, stepping over him with the okra. “Get up. You’re in my light.”

At noon EWTN rings the Angelus in the front room, and Mémère, on the daybed in her black with her ashes on and a blanket over her knees, says it along with the television in French, half a word ahead of the priest in Alabama. When it’s done she says something to Lena, and Lena lifts the lid of the old console and sets a record on it and puts the needle down, and Mahalia Jackson comes out of the speakers into the house, slow and enormous, like weather. Mémère closes her eyes to listen to it. She opens them on Jack, in the kitchen doorway, and crooks one finger.
He crosses. It’s four steps to the daybed. Lena comes up the hall with a sweater and stands in the far doorway of the front room with it folded over her arm.

Mémère has a holy card for him, its corners gone soft as cloth: Saint Joseph, with the lilies and the Child and a carpenter’s square at his feet. She turns it over to show him the back. The nineteenth of March is his birthday. Somebody in this house has been talking.

body.text:
SAINT JOSEPH · PRIEZ POUR NOUS
(on the back, in an old woman’s pencil) le 19 mars

body: She keeps hold of it after he’s taken it, so they’re both holding it, and talks. A good deal of it. Her French goes low and quick and level, the way she says the rosary, with Joseph’s name in it twice and a short dry laugh in the middle at somebody’s expense, and at the end she lets go of the card and taps his wrist with one finger and says one last thing, and is done.
Jack looks at the far doorway.
Lena shakes the sweater out and folds it again. “She says Joseph was a good man.”
He has been in this house eleven days. He knows about how long French runs in English. It doesn’t come out that short.

response: Mémère corrects his *r* — twice, the second time with her eyes shut, as if it pains her — and then pats his cheek two times with a hand like paper left out in the sun. In the hall doorway Lena holds the sweater against her stomach with both arms.

At half past one they eat the one meal at the oilcloth, Celeste’s shrimp and okra over rice and not a scrap of meat in the house, and Remy is given grace as a penance and gets lost in it between *bless us* and *bounty*. Tony comes in from the market in his apron, eats standing up at the counter, kisses his wife, and is back in the truck by two.
Lena folds the sweater again, though it’s already folded. “Drive safe.” She doesn’t look up from it.
Mémère looks from one of them to the other, and closes her eyes, and listens to Mahalia.

Tony comes in from Banks Street at twenty-five past one with ice on his cuffs and his apron still on under his jacket, and they eat at half past: Celeste’s shrimp and okra, no meat, the table quiet with hunger. Remy says grace and rushes it, and Celeste makes him say it again slower. By two the truck is gone back to the market and the pot is soaking in the sink.
Mémère, who understood that perfectly well in English, says, “*Menteur.*”
In the hall doorway Lena laughs without any sound at all, the sweater up over her mouth, and stops.

At half past one Remy says grace over Celeste’s shrimp and okra and finishes it, out of habit, with the prayer for the faithful departed. “Nobody’s dead, Remy,” Celeste says. “I am,” says Remy. Tony, in from the market, eats fast and says it’s the best she’s made, which he says every Ash Wednesday, and is gone again by two.

s05m.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:40 AM → 1:30 PM · BROUSSARD’S SEAFOOD, BANKS STREET — ICE
s05m.music: Mahalia Jackson — “Move On Up a Little Higher”
body: At twenty to ten on Ash Wednesday the line at Broussard’s goes out the door and along the front window and down Banks Street past the barbershop, and every forehead in it is marked. Some of the crosses are neat. Some are thumbprints. One, on a little boy holding a fistful of his grandmother’s coat, runs from his eyebrow up into his hair where he tried to rub it off and got caught. The sky over the street is low and white and hasn’t made up its mind about anything, and the bell over the door has quit ringing for each customer and settled into one long jangle.

Half of Mid-City is buying for Friday. Shrimp by the pound, heads on, in white paper. Catfish, whole and filleted. Crawfish for the weekend, the sacks by the walk-in door quieter than Monday’s. A man in a Knights of Columbus windbreaker wants forty pounds of drum for a fish fry at a church in Gentilly and wants it scaled, and Tony tells him scaled is Thursday, and the man says Thursday’s fine, and they shake on it over the case like two heads of state.

Tony works the register with the cordless phone jammed between his ear and his shoulder, writing Friday orders on the back of a paper sack with a carpenter’s pencil. There’s ice on the cuffs of his green market jacket and a smudge on his forehead, darker on the left where Hébert’s thumb pressed down. “Ten pounds, Mrs. Vo. Ten. No ma’am, I can’t hold you the big ones. It’s Lent. There’s no such thing as holding.”

Jack has the case. Gloria’s first rule is that nothing sits in its own water, and it holds on Banks Street the same as it holds over a Hobart in Marisol: he banks the shaved ice high at the back and low at the front, so the melt runs forward to the drain instead of pooling under the redfish, and lays the fish on it head to tail, and wraps, and weighs, and is back at the ice machine with the scoop every twenty minutes, because the case empties faster than he can fill it. The cotton gloves soak through by ten. By half past, his fingers have stopped reporting.

Under the front window Mr. Alcide opens oysters on his bench. The red radio on the shelf over him has WWOZ’s gospel hour on, and Mahalia Jackson is moving on up a little higher, slow, with the choir behind her, and Mr. Alcide goes right up with her in French, a half step behind and perfectly sure of himself.
At ten past eleven Miss Earline comes in under her plastic rain bonnet for a pound and the news. She gets the pound from Jack. She looks at his forehead while he wraps it.
“Father did yours,” she says.
“Yes ma’am.”

“I can tell. It leans to the Gospel side. Since Father came, every cross in this parish has had a little list to it.” She takes the shrimp and gives Tony the news across the register — the six o’clock was standing room, a Duplantis boy wore his Mardi Gras wig to it, the streetcar was full of dust — and then, with her change in her hand, looks back down the case at Jack. “And Lena’s going back out there with you.”
“Yes ma’am. All of us are.”
“Mm-hm,” says Miss Earline, and looks at Tony, and Tony looks at the register.
“You got your pound, Earline.”
“I got my pound,” she agrees, and ties her bonnet tighter under her chin, and goes out into the jangle with more news than she came in with.

Three and a half hours, and not one minute in them with room to think. He’s grateful. Ice, fish, paper, string, scale, the next one. Twice his right hand goes off on its own looking for the thing it has done after every hard hour since August, and finds the ice scoop instead, and he lets it have the scoop.

At a quarter past one Tony gives the register to the girl from the counter, a cousin of somebody’s, and comes down the length of the case wiping his hands on his apron, and tips his head at the walk-in. Jack follows him through the plastic strips. Tony pulls the steel door to behind them.

In here it’s February for real. One bulb in a wire cage, the compressor droning somewhere over their heads, boxes of Gulf shrimp packed in ice along the floor, and the drum laid out on its pallet, waiting for Thursday. The cold puts a little cloud in front of everything Tony says.

body.text: “Monday I asked you a question at the rail on Spanish Plaza in front of half of Mid-City.”
body.else: “Monday I asked you a question in this cooler.”

body: “I’m not asking it in my cooler.”
Jack’s hands are still wet from the case, and the cold goes straight into them. “I’d answer it if I could, Mr. Broussard.”
“I know you would.” Tony takes a crawfish sack off the stack, looks at it, and puts it back where it was. “That’s why I’m not asking.”
The compressor cuts out. In the quiet the sacks tick.

“I been watching phones all week,” Tony says. “Yours goes off, you take it out on the sidewalk. Hers goes off, she takes it out back by the shed and talks to the boil pot. Every time. I sell fish, son. I don’t do mysteries.”
There’s nothing Jack is allowed to say in here, and he doesn’t say it, and Tony nods at that like it was what he expected.

“Whatever it is you’re carrying,” Tony says, “and whoever’s on the end of it. You tell them to their face. Not on a phone. Not in a letter. Broussards do it to your face.” He points one thick finger at the floor of his own walk-in, the old knife scar white across the knuckle, as though the rule was poured in with the concrete.

He digs in his apron and comes out with a business card, and lays it flat against the steel wall, and writes on the back of it with the carpenter’s pencil from behind his ear, big square letters, bearing down hard enough to dent it.

—
FOR GLORIA. GULF SHRIMP, BROUSSARD PRICE. ASK FOR TONY.

body: He holds it out. “Who taught you ice? Gloria. You give her that.” He waits until it’s in Jack’s wet fingers. “Bring her.”

response: “Good.”
Tony puts his shoulder to the steel door and opens it on the warm and the line and Mahalia, and that’s the end of it. Jack dries the card on his shirt and puts it in his wallet behind his license.

At half past one Tony leaves the cousin the register and a list, hangs his apron on its nail, and drives Jack home to Dupre Street for the one meal with the heater on high and ice going to water on both their cuffs. He doesn’t say a word on the way. At the curb, with the engine running, he says, “I’ll be back for the van.”

choices.text: “I will, Mr. Broussard. To their face.”
response: Tony looks at him a long time in the cold, long enough for the little cloud in front of his mouth to come and go three times.
“Then you’re the only honest man in my cooler.”

Who, and when, he leaves alone. He picks up a box of shrimp and carries it out ahead of Jack through the plastic strips, and at half past one he has his apron off and the cousin on the phone and Jack in the truck, and he drives to Dupre Street one-handed with his other arm out the window in February, like a man who has been told the one thing he needed. At the stop sign on Orleans he says, “Three o’clock,” and taps the wheel with his wedding ring.

choices.text: “Is that the rule? Whoever works your case on Ash Wednesday —”
response: “— is mine. Yeah.” Tony shoulders the door open. “I’m making it up. It’s still the rule.”

He’s pleased with himself the rest of the afternoon. He tells the cousin at the register, and Mr. Alcide over the oysters, and at half past one, with his apron on the nail, he tells the truck. He laughs about it again at the light on Broad, and when he pulls up on Dupre Street he leans across Jack and opens his door for him. “Don’t let her leave without me.”

body: Laney opens the glovebox and puts Coco in it, fleur-de-lis up, and closes it with both hands.
“I am not riding two thousand miles with a coconut in front of my knees,” Theo says from the middle row.
“She’s not *a* coconut, Theodore.”

Margot goes up the porch steps to say goodbye to Mémère the way she would say goodbye to a department chair, hand out, and Mémère ignores the hand and pulls her down by it and kisses her on both cheeks. Margot submits with her arms at her sides and her glasses knocked crooked, and comes back down the steps a little pink, and gets into the passenger seat, and opens the atlas to Louisiana, and says, “That was not in the literature.”

Theo is sitting sideways in his chair with the door open and his sunglasses on, looking at the house. He has been up since before Jack was. He looks at the porch and the swing and the shed out back with its brown line around the boards at four and a half feet, the year the water came, and says, without taking the sunglasses off, “Eleven days. It was a Fellini picture. Three courses at every meal and somebody always singing.” There’s no topper. He keeps looking at the house.
Lena comes down the walk with her duffel and stops at the hatch, where Kevin is fitting the bags in by a system only he understands.
“Way-back,” she says.
Kevin clicks a pen and writes it at the bottom of the sheet without a word. Jack’s chair is the right one in the middle, where the sheet puts him.

Remy has come out on the porch in his sunglasses with a mug of black coffee, the one thing he’s allowed, and comes down off the steps to hug Jack one-armed, two slaps on the back, the second harder. “Forty days,” he says. “That’s what I gave. After that, Ohio, if you’re still —” He looks past Jack at the van, at the hatch, at his sister, and takes his sunglasses off and puts them back on. “Forty days.”

Luc is up, which is a surprise. He worked the Bourbon detail till two in the morning and he’s standing on the walk in a T-shirt and sweatpants with a coffee, and he shakes Jack’s hand once, the cop’s handshake, short and dry. “Drive the limit in Texas.” His eyes go to the open stretch of sidewalk between Jack and his sister at the side door, and rest there, and come back, and he drinks his coffee.
Jude stands in front of Jack with his perfect cross and his book bag still on both shoulders.

body: “Tuesday,” Jack says.
Jude thinks about it and nods, man to man, and hitches his book bag up and goes inside, satisfied.
Josie has the porch rail. She sits on it with her knees up and her gray sleeve and her eyes on the curb.

body.text: “We’re not at the table now.”
“You’re not in college *now*. You’re on the curb.”
“You looked at your plate. I saw.”

Laney stops with the shoe polish. Kevin stops with a bag. At the van’s side door Lena goes on fitting her small bag in under the way-back seat, and it takes her exactly as long as it would have taken anyway.

She does. She takes a pen out of her uniform pocket and writes it on the back of her hand, EASTER, in letters that get smaller toward the knuckles, and blows on it, and holds it up at him so he can see it’s official.

She isn’t angry. She holds up three fingers at him from the rail and folds them down one at a time, keeping the book, and when she gets to the fist she looks at it as though the answer might be in there after all.

Josie, on the rail, translates every word. “She says the dust looks good on you.” She listens to the rest. “She says it’s the first honest thing you’ve worn all week.”
Mémère lets go of his sleeve and folds her hands on the blanket, and that’s the last word on it, in either language.

She looks at the two of them, him at the porch steps and her daughter at the far end of the van with her hand on the side door, and says, “Hm.”

body: Lena goes back up the walk. Jack stands at the van’s open door, out of the way, and watches the Broussards say goodbye to her.

Celeste holds her by the back of the head and says something into her hair that nobody else is meant to hear, and nobody does. Mémère reaches up from the chair and puts her fingertips on the medal on its mended chain, and keeps them there a while, her lips moving. Tony picks her up off the porch step under the arms like she’s nine years old and a king just waved at her off a float, and sets her down a step lower, and wipes his face with the back of his wrist. The twins come down the walk on either side of her, at her elbows, Josie talking and Jude not.

She has washed her face. Jack can see the water still at her hairline. She washed all of it but her forehead, and the cross Hébert put there is still there, crooked to the Gospel side. She gets into the van by the far door and climbs over into the way-back without a look at the middle row.

Kevin turns the key. The whole house is on the porch: Celeste with her arms folded, Tony with his hand up, Mémère in her chair, Remy on the steps, Luc in the doorway with his coffee, Jude beside him, Josie up on the rail. And Clovis, leaning on the porch post with a Kool behind his ear he isn’t lighting till they’re gone, starts the first verse of “Just a Closer Walk with Thee,” off-key and slow, as Kevin pulls away from the curb, and the rest of the porch doesn’t join in, because Clovis knows the first verse of everything and the rest of nothing, and the porch has learned to let him.

In the side mirror the clothesline in the side yard goes by, and on it, pinned by their rolled tops, the gold bags from Fat Tuesday in a row, LARGE among them, turning a little on the line in the wind with their eyeholes.

s07.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:30 PM · I-10 WEST, THE MISSISSIPPI AT BATON ROUGE — FORTY DAYS
body: The bridge at Baton Rouge goes up over the river in a long gray hump, and the Mississippi goes by under it brown and wide and indifferent, the other way from last time, and then they’re down on the far side among the cane fields, cut to stubble now, the color gone out of everything but the sky.

Kevin drives with both hands. Margot has the passenger seat and the atlas open on her knees to Louisiana, though they won’t need it till El Paso. Theo and Jack have the two middle chairs. Laney and Lena have the way-back. The radio is off and stays off. It’s a van full of people after Mass, the quiet on the church steps before anybody lights up or says what they thought of the homily, and Jack, who has nothing to light, sits in it with his hands between his knees, rubbing his thumb back and forth along the seam of his jeans until the denim is warm.
Every forehead in the van is smudged.
“Okay,” Laney says from the back. “Okay, okay, okay. It’s up.” She leans forward between the middle chairs and holds her pink BlackBerry up over the seats so the van can see it.
