body: “Tagging y’all,” Laney says.
“Don’t tag me,” Lena says.
“Why.”
“I won’t see it.”
There’s a small silence in the way-back. “…*Why* won’t you see it.”
“I gave it up.”
Laney lowers the phone.

“I’m sorry,” she says. “I’m sorry, I just — no. No ma’am. You don’t give up *Facebook*. People give up chocolate. People give up *Diet Coke*. Facebook is the *news*, Magdalena. What you’re describing is a *disappearance*. It’s witness protection. Forty days! Do you know what happens in forty days? People get engaged in forty days. People get *divorced*. Somebody’s going to have a baby and you won’t know if it’s a boy. Somebody’s going to change their —” She stops. “— their *picture*, and you’re going to walk around Marisol like Rip Van Winkle in a mantilla. How are you going to *know* anything? How is anybody going to know you *know*? This is the most selfish thing I have ever heard of a Catholic doing, and I took AP European History.”

Margot has the visor down against the sun, which is low and straight ahead now and will be till dark, and in the little mirror on the back of it Jack can see Theo’s face, and behind it, from the way-back, Laney’s. Their eyes meet in the glass. It lasts no time at all. Jack keeps his face where it is, and in the rearview, past Kevin’s ear, Lena is keeping hers.
Lena folds her hands on her knees.

“It’s Facebook,” she says, the way she’d read a docket. “It’s every Friday on bread and water, the old way. It’s the Stations at St. Brendan’s, every Friday night. That’s my Lent. It isn’t up for discussion, and it isn’t up for comment.”
“Bread and water’s not the minimum, Lena,” Kevin says.
“I’m not a minimum kind of girl, Kevin.”

“Durkheim has a name for this.” Margot doesn’t look up from Louisiana. “The negative cult. The rites of abstention. What you won’t eat, what you won’t say, what you won’t do on which days. You’ve all agreed to be holier by subtraction.” She turns a page to Texas. “It’s very efficient.”
“Aquinas gives three reasons to fast,” Lena says. “To bridle the flesh. To lift the mind. To make satisfaction for sin. Durkheim found the first one and called it the whole cult.”
“Durkheim was a rabbi’s son. I imagine he fasted plenty.” Margot turns another page. “Then he stopped, and wrote it up.”
“Then he knew what it costs, and he still called it a rite.” In the rearview Jack can see a slice of her: one eye, the ash, the window behind her going by. “Good. It is one. Write that up.”
“And you got ashes,” Theo says.
“Fieldwork has a dress code.”
“Sweets,” Kevin says, unprompted, in the voice he uses for medical histories. “No sweets until Easter. Bà Nội’s rule, since I was seven. Family history of it.”
“Carbs,” Laney says, sitting back. “In solidarity. I’m a lapsed Baptist, I don’t have to give up a thing, so it counts *double*.” A pause. “Until Phoenix.”
“Phoenix is tomorrow,” says Margot.
“Then it’s going to be a very *intense* Lent.”
Theo has his forehead against the window, watching a crop duster’s hangar go by in a field of nothing. “Kevin says I already gave something up.”
Kevin drives. His eyes stay on the road, and the road stays straight.
“What about you, Father Jack?” Theo says, his forehead still on the glass.
“Cigarettes.”
“We *know*,” says Laney. “Louisiana knows.”
And there are Fridays.

Lent on Glenwood Avenue was Mrs. Paul’s fish sticks and a can of peas, and the fish fry in the basement at St. Brigid’s with Frank at a folding table eating three plates of perch because it was the only time all year a Costigan got to be pious and full at once. On Glenwood Avenue bread and water was for the Little Flower and the Desert Fathers. Nonna did it, in Calabria, as a girl, and told it like a war story. He hasn’t eaten since the shrimp and okra and his stomach knows it, and his hands want the thing they want, and somewhere behind him a girl just read her Lent into the record like she was daring God to find a hole in it, and he hasn’t said his Fridays to anybody yet.

choices.key: On the drive home you said out loud you’d fast every Friday of Lent on bread and water, the way Lena does.
response: From the way-back, her eyes on her own hands: “Nobody asked you, Youngstown.”

“Oh, *Lord*,” Laney says. “It’s a *competition*.” She flops back against the seat with her phone face down on her stomach, her Lent personally ruined by both of them, and in the rearview Lena is looking out the back glass at Louisiana going away behind WHO DAT, with the corner of her mouth exactly where it was.

choices.key: On the drive home you decided, without telling anybody, to fast every Friday of Lent on bread and water.
response: He doesn’t say it. He decides it, there in the middle chair with the cane fields going by, bread and water every Friday till Easter, and it’s devotion and it’s pride, both at once, the wanting to give God something and the wanting to keep up with her, and he can’t pull one out of the other and doesn’t try. He’ll take that one to a priest. Behind him, in the way-back, Laney is explaining to Lena how a person could check Facebook *only for emergencies*, and Lena is saying no.

choices.text: “Bread and water. That’s a Tuesday in Ohio.”
choices.key: On the drive home you told the van you’d do bread and water on Fridays too, and called it a Tuesday in Ohio.
response: Theo laughs into the window. Laney says, “He’s *joking*. Look at him. He’s not joking.”

From the way-back, nothing. Not even *Youngstown*. He looks in the rearview, and she’s looking out the back glass at the river going away behind WHO DAT, and the nothing goes on past the next exit, and he feels all of it.

s08.slug: WEDNESDAY · 5:45 PM · THE ATCHAFALAYA BASIN BRIDGE — WASH YOUR FACE
body: Past Baton Rouge the land goes wet and then gives up, and the interstate climbs onto its concrete legs and stays there, two spans side by side running out over the Basin for eighteen miles, with the sun dead ahead of them now and going. There’s no heron this time. The water under the cypress is empty and black, and the light drains out of it from the bottom up while the treetops keep a little copper.

Kevin drives with the visor down and his eyes narrowed to slits. Theo has the other middle chair, his loafers off and his socked feet up on the console between them. In the way-back Laney is typing with both thumbs, a steady plastic clicking, and Lena is somewhere behind Jack’s headrest, where he can’t see her without turning around, and he doesn’t turn around.
The RAZR goes off in his breast pocket, alone in there, against the place the tin wore into the lining. SKYE (MISFIT).
“Hey,” he says.
“Hi.”
Just her, first thing, with nobody in front of her; he doesn’t know what to make of that, and then she’s going.

“I’m in my trailer in a robe with my hair in forty pins. I have twelve minutes, and there’s a wig on a foam head on the counter watching me like it’s heard things. Tonight a truck rains on me again. Show me your dirt.”
“My what?”
“Your *dirt*, Jack. Your ashes. It’s been Wednesday all day where you are, and I want to see it before you sweat it off or Ted licks his thumb and fixes it. Picture. Now. I’ll hold.”

He turns the RAZR around in his hand so the little lens on the hinge looks back at him and holds it out at the end of his arm, aiming at nothing he can see. The first one is the van’s headliner and half an eyebrow. The second is his nose and a piece of Louisiana. Across the aisle Theo leans over with a helpful hand out. “The subject doesn’t —”
“I’ve got it.”

The third one has it: one eye squinted against the sun, and over it Father Hébert’s thumb, a gray cross leaning left like a fence post after a Youngstown winter. *New Picture Msg.* He sends it and puts the phone back to his ear and waits.
What comes out of the RAZR is a shriek, loud enough that the van hears it and Kevin’s eyes come up to the mirror.
“Is she okay?” Kevin says.
“She got the picture.”

“Oh, *look* at you. Hold still. Madame Skye will read it.” And there she is after all, a boardwalk booth with a beaded curtain, bangles going on both wrists. “Madame Skye sees… a long journey. Many miles. A van. A coconut — why is there a coconut —”
“Long story.”
“Madame Skye charges by the minute. She sees a man in a dress —”
“Vestments.”

“A man in a *robe*, forgive me, Father. An old man. His thumb, it shakes.” The bangles slow. “But he pressed hard. Look at that. He leaned in.” Madame goes back behind her curtain, and it’s Skye, in a trailer in Burnaby, looking at a stamp-sized picture of his face. “That’s a good thumb, Jack. That man meant it.”
“He’s seventy-four.”
“He meant it at seventy-four. That’s harder. What did he say when he did it?”
“Remember that you are dust, and to dust you will return.” He looks at the cypress going by. “Then he said something in French.”
“What did he say in French?”
“*Le garçon de l’Ohio.* The boy from Ohio.”
“He *knows* you.”
“He’s met me twice.”

“Twice is plenty, for a man who leans in.” Paper rustles on her end; she has printed something out again. “Okay. Real question. I read it, the one they read today, Matthew six. I found it on a church website with a dove that flaps its wings when you scroll. It’s the only scripture with a makeup note. *Wash your face, so nobody can tell you’re fasting.* And then you all walk around all day with dirt on it. Explain it.”
He knows exactly how small the van is, how well a voice carries in it from the middle chairs to the back. He answers her anyway, because she asked it straight.

“The fast is the part nobody sees,” he says. “That’s Matthew six. That’s between you and Him, so you keep your face clean and it stays that way. The ashes aren’t that. The ashes don’t say *look how holy I am*. They say *I’m going to die*. Remember you’re dust. And everybody gets the same thumb — the bishop, the lady from the dry cleaner’s, the guy with the bad hip in the back pew. You don’t pick it out, and you can’t do it well.” He looks for the rest and finds it in his father’s mouth. “My dad says when Campbell Works was still running, every man on the shift came out the gate the same gray. Nobody at the bar after thought the soot made you a good steelworker. It just meant you’d been in there with everybody else. And you wash it off at night. It’s not supposed to make it to tomorrow.”
Behind him, in the way-back, the clicking has stopped.
Skye is quiet. Then: “So it’s a costume that isn’t allowed to be a performance.”
“Yes.”
“That’s the hardest note there is.”
“Kyle’s doing Lent, by the way. He’s giving up the Colts. He came into the makeup trailer this morning and said it to the mirror like a wedding vow. Russ cried. I think Russ cried.”
“Is Kyle Catholic?”
“Kyle is from Fort Wayne. It’s close.” A pin goes into something on her end. “I’m doing it too,” she says. “Lent.”
“What are you giving up?”
“Matthew six, Jack. I read the fine print.”
He waits, and she lets him wait, and he can hear her enjoying it.

body.text: “Also. You told me to go be brilliant. I was brilliant. Ask the goose. The goose was there for all six hours. The goose wept.”
body.else: “Also. The goose saw your bag picture. The goose thinks it’s a cry for help.”

body.text: “And I’ve started the binder. It has tabs.”
“What’s on the tabs?”
“Fridays. Cigarettes. Loopholes. Loopholes is the thickest tab.”
“Did you say one for me this morning?”
“I offered the whole thing.”
“The *what*?”
“Lent. All of it.”
On her end, nothing at all. Then: “Well. Okay. That’s a lot of Lent.”
“Did you say one for me this morning?”
“I did.”
“A good one?”
“On my knees on a kneeler older than my dad.”
“Good. I said I’d hold you to it.”
“So. For real this time?”
“For real.”
“Good. I’m holding you to it. I have a very strong grip. Ask anybody I’ve ever shaken hands with at a premiere.”

body: She brings the phone in close; he can tell by the way the trailer goes away behind her. “Wash it off tonight,” she says, low, right against his ear. “Like the book says. And Tuesday you come down the hill clean, and I’m going to find out if any of it comes off on my pillowcase.”
Tuesday. She has it written down somewhere in that trailer, in a hand he’d know anywhere. He looks out at the black water going by under the bridge.
“I’m in a van, Skye.”
“I know. I can hear Ted breathing through his mouth.”
Across the aisle Theo shuts his mouth.
He loves her. It’s as much a fact as the bridge, concrete under all six of them.
Behind him, low, Laney says something to the way-back, and gets no answer.
On her end someone knocks and says a number through a door. “That’s me,” Skye says, and then, fast: “Six days. I’m counting. I don’t count.” A little sound, the robe or the pins. “Bye, Dust.”

choices.key: On the Atchafalaya bridge Skye called to see your ashes and told you she was keeping a Lent of her own. “Six days,” you said.
response: “Six days,” he says.
“Six,” she says, and is gone. He keeps the shut phone in his fist until the bridge comes down onto dry land.

choices.text: “Whatever you’re giving up — it’s a good present.”
choices.key: On the Atchafalaya bridge Skye called to see your ashes and told you she was keeping a Lent of her own. You told her whatever she was giving up, it was a good present.
response: “Whatever you’re giving up,” he says, “it’s a good present.”
On her end the knock comes again, and she lets it. “Okay,” she says, just that, and the line goes. The RAZR sits shut on his knee, warm from his ear.

choices.key: On the Atchafalaya bridge Skye called to see your ashes and told you she was keeping a Lent of her own. You gave her back her old goodbye, and she laughed.
response: “Bye, Coat check.”
She laughs, startled, right into the dial tone.

s08a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:15 PM · HOUSTON, A GAS STATION OFF I-10
body: Through Lafayette nobody says much. In the rearview, past Kevin’s ear, Lena has her face turned to the window and the dark going by in it, and Laney’s hand is on her knee, and at Lake Charles the hand is still there.

On the west side of Houston, Kevin brings them in under a canopy lit so white it takes the color out of everybody: twelve pumps, a store that’s a wall of glass, a man in a Texans cap filling a bass boat. Jack takes the nozzle. Through the glass, on a television bracketed over the cigarette rack, a snowboarder goes up a wall of snow with his hair out behind him, turns over in the air, lands, and goes up again, the sound off.
Lena comes around the back of the van with her LG in her hand, lit. On its outside screen, small and white: JULIAN.
She looks at it. She walks past the pumps to the ice machine at the end of the store, turns her back to the island, and answers it.

Four minutes by the clock over the door. He can see all of it and hear none of it: her free hand pushed down into the jean jacket’s pocket, her head down, the ice machine’s blue sign on her hair. Once she nods. Once she puts her hand on the ice machine’s lid and leaves it there. The pump clicks off. He hangs up the nozzle and screws the cap on and waits for the receipt, and the receipt takes its time.
She shuts the phone and comes back across the concrete and climbs into the way-back past Laney’s knees, and says nothing, and nobody asks her anything.
Margot holds out her hand for the keys. On Kevin’s sheet, taped to the dash, the next line says MARGOT: Houston → San Antonio.

s09.slug: THURSDAY · 2:40 AM · I-10 WEST, PAST SONORA — THE NAVIGATOR
body: Kevin’s sheet gives Jack San Antonio to Fort Stockton and gives the seat beside him to Theo. West of Junction the Hill Country lets go of its hills one at a time, and out here past Sonora there’s nothing left for the headlights to find but the white line and the bar ditch, and now and then two green coins low in the ditch that don’t blink and don’t move — a deer — and then they’re behind him. The cruise is set at seventy-two. The dash clock is the only light in the van that isn’t the road’s.

Theo has the atlas on his knees, open to Texas, a church bulletin keeping Arizona. Jack looks at it there. The last time it was three in the morning in Texas, that atlas rode on somebody else’s knees, going the other way.

Everybody else is asleep. Kevin is folded across a middle chair with his windbreaker over his face. Margot sleeps upright against her window with her mouth shut, declining to comment even unconscious. In the way-back Laney is a heap of pashmina with the coconut’s crown sticking out of it, and beside her Lena lies on her side with her knees drawn up. A truck goes by the other way, and its lights come through the van and lift her face out of the dark in the rearview — gray, eyes shut — and put it back. That’s all the mirror tells him.
He has had the sentence since Lake Charles. He has turned it over so many times crossing Texas that the corners have worn off it, and it still isn’t any lighter.
Theo is awake. Theo is usually awake at this hour; in 412 it’s the laptop light on his face at two and three, and here it’s the dash, green.
“Is the coconut legal in California,” Theo says, eventually.
“It’s dead. It’s painted.”

“It’s a fruit, Costigan. There’s an inspection station at Blythe. Laney’s been rehearsing since Baton Rouge.” Theo puts his head back against the rest. “Picture it. A checkpoint at dusk. A woman in sunglasses. A coconut in sequins, with everything to lose.”
“It’s not a checkpoint.”
“Tell Coco.”
“How’s Hale?”
“One sentence.”
“Four thousand words due Monday, and you have one sentence.”
“It’s a good sentence.”
“He’ll have it framed,” Theo says. “Then he’ll fail you under the frame.”
Somewhere past Ozona Theo says he doesn’t understand how they score the snowboarding, and Jack says he saw some of it through a window in Houston and doesn’t either, and that’s the Olympics.

West of the next exit a doe comes up out of the bar ditch and stands in the right lane, gray in the high beams, her ears turned toward them. Jack is off the cruise and standing on the brake, and the van noses down and everything loose in it slides forward, and the doe takes two long unhurried steps and is over the median and gone. Theo has one hand braced on the dash. Behind them Kevin says something into his windbreaker and doesn’t wake. Jack eases back up through sixty and seventy and sets the cruise again, and his heart goes on banging a long time after, like somebody at a door.

Then nothing for a long time: the tires, the heater, the white line coming at them out of the dark and going under. The radio is on scan, and on scan out here it mostly finds static and a man selling feed, until a station somewhere in West Texas comes up clear with Emmylou Harris on it, and the scan stops there. Theo reaches over and turns it down. Not off.

“‘Boulder to Birmingham,’” he says. “She wrote it after Gram Parsons died. He died out in the desert, at Joshua Tree, and his friends stole the body out of the airport and drove it back out there and burned it. Because he’d asked them to.”
“That’s a true story?”
“Hand to God.” Theo looks at the radio. “Some people get a friend like that.”
They listen to a verse of it. Jack checks the mirror. The way-back is dark, and nothing moves in it, and he looks at the road again.
“Theo.”
“Costigan.”
“I’m ending it with Skye. Tuesday. When she’s back.”
It’s the first time he’s said it to anyone but her. It sounds smaller in the van than it did in his head, and truer, and it can’t be put back.
Theo turns his head and looks out his window. There’s nothing out there. He looks at it anyway, for as long as the song takes to get to its chorus and past it.
“Okay,” he says.
And after a while: “Okay.”
Jack waits. The next question is right there in the van with them, close enough to pick up off the dash, and Theo turns around in his seat and looks straight at it and doesn’t ask it.
“Don’t tell me anything else.”
“I wasn’t going to.”
“Good.” Theo faces front. “Don’t.”
His iPhone is on his thigh. He wakes it, and his thumb opens something, and hangs over the glass, and types nothing. He locks it and turns it face down on his leg.
Jack watches the white line. Theo has shut the atlas on his own finger and left it there.
A few miles on, a blue sign comes up with a picnic table on it.
“Pull off.”
“You okay?”
“Pull off, Costigan.”

It’s three concrete tables under three tin roofs and a windbreak of cedars all leaning the same way, and nobody. Jack pulls in and stops with the headlights on the cedars. Theo gets out, and the cold comes in where he was, and he walks out past the tables, past the end of the light, and stops. Jack can just make him out: his back to the van, both hands on top of his head with the fingers laced, the way guys stood at the foul line at the rec center after the last game of a bad season.

He stands like that a minute. The engine ticks. When Jack leans to look up through the windshield, the sky over the cedars is crowded down to the ground. Jack keeps his hands on the wheel. He could get out. He doesn’t; Theo walked a long way into the dark to stand with his back to the van. In the way-back nobody stirs. Emmylou goes on low to the cedars, and gets to the end, and the station goes back to a man reading the weather for Pecos County.
Theo comes back across the light with his hands in his blazer pockets and gets in and shuts the door and puts his belt on.
“Leg cramp,” he says.

Jack puts it in drive. Out on the interstate a westbound rig goes by with every running light it owns lit up, amber and red all down its length, a carnival with somewhere to be, and is gone up the road.
They’re back up to seventy-two when Theo says, “She’s —”
“I know.”
“Callender’s going to —”
“I know, Theo.”
“She sent me a picture of your violets,” Theo says. “On Sunday. In the trailer. No caption.” He stops there.

Theo rubs his eyes with the heels of both hands. He has known her since they were kids under the craft-services table on the Meridian lots, rating everybody’s outfits; he has been her Ted longer than Jack has been anybody’s anything.
“Be good to her,” Theo says. “Tuesday. Just — be good to her.”

choices.text: “I will. She gets the truth, the whole thing, to her face. It’s the best thing I’ve got.”
choices.key: Past Sonora at a quarter to three in the morning you told Theo you’re ending it with Skye on Tuesday. That was all you told him. You promised him she’d get the whole truth, to her face.
response: “I will,” Jack says. “She gets the truth. The whole thing, to her face. It’s the best thing I’ve got.”
Theo nods at the windshield. “It is,” he says. “It’s the best thing you’ve got.” The weather man gives the wind for Pecos County, and neither of them says anything over it.

choices.text: “I love her, Theo. That’s the part that doesn’t help.”
choices.key: Past Sonora at a quarter to three in the morning you told Theo you’re ending it with Skye on Tuesday. That was all you told him — and that you love her, and it doesn’t help.
response: “I love her, Theo,” he says. “That’s the part that doesn’t help.”
“No,” Theo says. “It never does.” He opens the atlas again and finds where they are in the dash light with one finger, a blue line in a lot of white, and looks at it, and closes it.

choices.text: “You took me to that party. I’m putting it on your tab.”
choices.key: Past Sonora at a quarter to three in the morning you told Theo you’re ending it with Skye on Tuesday. That was all you told him. You put it on his tab.
response: “You took me to that party,” Jack says. “I’m putting it on your tab.”

“I owe you a kidney,” Theo says. It’s meant for a joke and doesn’t land as one, and neither of them tries another. Around five the lights of Fort Stockton come up out of the flat ahead, a handful of orange on the black, and Theo points at them without a word.

choices.key: Past Sonora at a quarter to three in the morning you told Theo you’re ending it with Skye on Tuesday. That was all you told him. Then you drove.
response: Jack nods, and drives. Seventy-two on the cruise. The white line coming and going under. Beside him Theo reaches over and turns the radio back up one notch, and that’s the end of talking till Fort Stockton.

s10.slug: THURSDAY · 7:40 AM · FORT STOCKTON, A TRUCK STOP OFF I-10 — THE FOURTEENTH MORNING
body: They pulled in at five, per the sheet, and everybody slept two hours across the seats but Jack and Theo.

Now the sun is up over the flat behind them, low and white, and every rig in the lot throws a shadow a hundred feet long toward New Mexico. It’s the dry cold of the high desert in February, the kind that goes through denim like it isn’t there. Kevin stands at the driver’s door doing hamstring stretches with the keys already in his fist. Lena is at the back bumper with a coffee in both hands and her hood up, out of the wind, at the edge of everything.
In the men’s room Jack washes his face at a steel sink, and the last of Wednesday comes off his hairline gray and goes down the drain.

Margot sits sideways in the passenger seat with the door open and her boots on the running board and a paperback on her knee. When he comes back across the lot she holds out the Gideon without looking up from her page: small, green, worn to the weave at the corners, SANTA LUCIA MOTOR COURT stamped purple inside the board. The fourteenth morning.

He doesn’t need it. He leans on the van’s cold flank and says it into the cold from memory — *He summoned the Twelve and began to send them out two by two* — the staff and the sandals, *no food, no sack, no money in their belts*, with Gloria’s ones folded in the wallet against his hip, and the dust at the end, shaken off your feet. He hands the book back. Margot takes it with her eyes still on the paperback and puts it in her coat.

His hands won’t stay anywhere. He has a bottle of water from inside, and he takes the label off it in strips with his thumbnail, one, then the next, till it’s bare, and starts on the glue. He cracks his knuckles, all of them, twice. He drums on the roof rack until Laney, inside, says “*Please*,” and then he drums on his own leg. Under the skin on the insides of his forearms something crawls that scratching can’t get to, and he scratches anyway. The coffee is his second and hasn’t touched the fog. And under all of it is the want — not a cigarette so much as the business of one, the cellophane coming off in one pull, the flick, the first drag going down to the bottom of him — so exact he can taste the filter. Every fight he’s had since August ended there. He has a fight in him right now and nowhere to put it.

Kevin watches him over the top of the driver’s door. “It’s not the nicotine,” he says. “You smoke like it’s a holy day of obligation. It’s the hands — the habit’s been told no.” He swings up into the seat. “Textbook. Tired and hungry makes it worse. Respectfully, you’re a hazard to navigation.”
“He’s not a patient, Kevin,” Laney says from inside.
“Everybody’s a patient, Laney.” Kevin adjusts his mirror. “Some of us are just in the waiting room.”

To give his hands a job, Jack gets out Hale’s legal pad and sits on the step of the open side door with it on his knee: THE SECOND LINE across the top, the one good sentence under it, and the bottom of the pad ragged where six strips came off in an attic in Mid-City. He clicks the pen. His hand wants to be doing something else, and he makes it do this instead, and starts the second paragraph.

body.text: *Then a trumpet player found me in the crowd and pointed the bell at me, as though the song had been looking for the man worst at it, to make him go first.*
body.else: *From the curb you can watch the second line go by and believe it has nothing to do with you, which is what curbs are for.*

body: Theo comes around the front of the van with Coco under his arm like a football and a coffee in his other hand. “Fun fact,” he says. “She’s not technically a nut. She’s a drupe. Laney should lead with that at Blythe. It’s a completely different —”
“Nobody cares, Theo.” Jack doesn’t look up from the pad. “Nobody in this van has cared about one thing out of your mouth since August that wasn’t about you.”

He hears it land. Theo stands there with the coconut and the coffee. Then he sets the coffee on the van’s roof, very carefully, and presses the lid down around its rim, though there was nothing wrong with the lid.
By the back bumper, Lena, with her own coffee in both hands, looks at the ground.

response: “Sorry, Theo,” he says. “That wasn’t you.”

“It was a little me.” Theo takes his coffee down off the roof and hands Jack the coconut to hold while he climbs in. It’s generous, and quick, and Jack sits there on the step holding a painted coconut, forgiven before he’s finished being ashamed.

choices.text: “I’d like to apologize to the coconut.”
response: “I’d like to apologize to the coconut,” he says.
From inside the van, Laney: “*She* accepts.” Theo takes his coffee down off the roof and climbs in past him with Coco. He doesn’t say whether he does.

He bends over the pad. Theo stands there a second longer; then he takes his coffee down off the roof and gets in with the coconut and lets it go, and Jack would rather have been hit. He writes half a page he’ll cross out in El Paso.

s11.slug: THURSDAY · 10:20 AM · EL PASO, A GAS STATION OFF I-10 — THE AIR PUMP
body: “We gained an hour,” Kevin says, past Van Horn, when the dash clock and the RAZR stop agreeing. He reaches over and sets the clock back with the tip of a pen. “I’m logging it.”
By El Paso Jack has two pages.

It’s the same station. He knows it from the off-ramp: six islands under the canopy, chain-link past the last of them, and below the grade of the interstate the concrete channel with the line down the middle and Juárez on the other side, poured up the side of its mountain, which at midnight was a lamp left on and at ten in the morning is just a city, tan and pink and enormous, with laundry on its roofs. The square of cardboard is still taped over the card reader on pump four. PAY INSIDE AFTER 10 PM. Kevin reads it aloud anyway.

At the edge of the lot, where the concrete gives out into gravel, is the air pump. Jack doesn’t look at it. He knows where it is without looking. The seventeenth rides in a tin in her jacket now, dated in his hand; she was asleep in the van forty feet from it when he lit it, and didn’t know till the levee.

Inside, the store’s radio is on an El Paso station, or a Juárez one, and Selena is singing “Como la Flor” over the hot-dog rollers, and the woman at the register sings the end of every line along with her, a hair behind. Jack pours a coffee. He puts the lid on. He sets it on the counter, and he hears himself ask for a pack of Marlboro Reds before he knows he’s going to, the way you’d hear somebody behind you in line.

Behind her the cigarettes stand in their slots up the wall, every brand in its row like bolts in a hardware bin. She takes a red box down from its slot by feel and puts it on the counter. “¿Algo más?” — “No. Gracias.” His Spanish is the Anchor’s dish pit, Rudy’s, about forty words and most of them about pans. Five and change. He pays out of the fold of Gloria’s ones in his wallet, his fingers not quite steady on them, counting them out face up and all facing one direction: Gloria’s rule for tips.

He walks out with the coffee in one hand and the pack in the other. At pump four Kevin has the hood up and is reading the dipstick in the sun, and Margot is doing the windshield with the squeegee in long exact strokes, and Laney is asleep against the back glass with her mouth open. He walks past all of it, across the lot, and stands under the air pump.

Nobody’s using it. AIR 75¢, and the hose hanging in a loop off its hook, and under it a dark ring on the concrete where cars have dripped for years. Thirteen days ago he stood on that ring at five to midnight and lit the last one.

Through the store’s open door Selena is still going. Rudy keeps a radio over the fryer at the Anchor tuned to a station out of Oxnard, and on Saturday nights Jack has scraped a few thousand plates to this song without ever knowing what it was called, and here it is, in El Paso, where it belongs.

He sets the coffee on top of the pump. The pack is lighter than he remembers and heavier than it should be. The cellophane is tight and cold and takes the sun. The red tear strip runs around under the lid with its little tab standing up, waiting for a thumbnail. He can smell it through the plastic, or thinks he can — the sweet brown smell that lived in his father’s truck and in the Carhartt and at the end of every argument he ever walked out of. His thumbnail finds the tab and rests there.

His hands are still. All morning they’ve been at the label on a water bottle and the roof rack and his own knuckles, and now, with this in them, they’re quiet as a sleeping dog, and that’s the worst thing he’s found out about himself in Texas.
He doesn’t open it.

If it’s in his pocket, he chooses every hour, all the way to Easter. If it’s in the trash can by the door, he’s at the next exit buying another, and he knows that about himself as well as he knows anything.
Theo comes out of the store with two coffees, sees Jack already has one, and stops. He sees what’s in Jack’s other hand.
“Costigan —”
“I’m not opening it.”
Theo stands there in the sun with a coffee in each hand. “…Okay.” He looks past Jack at the van, at its open side door, and back, and whatever he sees there he keeps.

The van’s side door is open. Lena sits on its step with her jean jacket buttoned to the neck and her hands in its pockets, and she has seen all of it, from the counter through the glass to the air pump; he can see on her that she has. Her face is turned his way, and very still. The wind off the channel blows her hair across her face, and she lets it.

body.text: In his wallet, behind his father’s folded note, a strip of yellow legal pad says *Wed 2/17 · Lent*. He doesn’t take it out.

response: He walks it over to the side door and holds it out to her, in the cold, at the length of his arm.
She looks at it. Her hands stay in her pockets.
“No,” Lena says. “You bought it. You carry it.”
He stands there with it held out a moment longer. Then the pack goes into the Carhartt’s breast pocket, in beside the phone, and he does up the button, and she watches him do the button.

“A man buys cigarettes to prove he doesn’t smoke,” says Theo. “Bresson would weep.” He hands over the second coffee anyway, and Jack, a coffee in each hand now, gets the hair shirt into his breast pocket on the third try, wedged in behind the RAZR.

s11a.slug: THURSDAY · 10:35 AM · EL PASO — THE SIDE WINDOW
body: The side door rolls shut on its track with Lena inside. Jack has the nozzle in pump four, the numbers turning over, and the store’s radio has gone on to somebody selling tires in Spanish.

body.text: Through the van’s side window she lifts one hand with all five fingers spread, and holds it up there, and puts it down, and looks at the road.
body.else: Through the glass she looks at the pack in his breast pocket for a long time, and then at the road.

body: The pump clicks off. Kevin, at the driver’s door, counts heads through the glass with one finger and gets five, because Laney has the coconut up in the window. The pack rides where he put it, unopened, square against him under the canvas; once, as he hangs up the nozzle, his hand goes up to the flap and finds the button done, and comes away.

Out the back glass, past WHO DAT, the air pump gets small, and then the station, and then Juárez is a tan smear across the channel and gone behind an overpass. Out of El Paso the interstate bends north along the river, and a green sign comes up on the right: LAS CRUCES 44. Past it the Organ Mountains stand up out of the desert in a row of gray spires, the pipes of a church the size of New Mexico, which is the joke somebody already made when they named them. The pad is on his knee. Page three.

s12.slug: THURSDAY · 2:15 PM · TEXAS CANYON REST AREA, I-10, ARIZONA — THE BOULDERS
body: In daylight Texas Canyon looks like the end of a game somebody quit in a temper. Granite boulders the size of sheds and the size of houses lie heaped up both slopes of the pass, round as loaves, one balanced on two with nothing holding it up there but the fact that it hasn’t come down yet. The wind comes through the rest area at a steady lean, under the ramadas and over the concrete tables, and gets into anything that isn’t held down: napkins, the trash-can liners, Laney’s hair, the pages of a legal pad. The Odyssey sits nose-in at the end of the lot with WHO DAT · 40 DAYS on the back glass in Laney’s white shoe polish, and the sun is on everything and warms none of it.
Two Fridays ago they came through here after dark, and he was shouting a January phone call back at her word for word, and he never saw a single rock.

He has a picnic table to himself. He sits up on the tabletop with his boots on the bench, which is the only way to get his knees high enough for Hale’s legal pad, and he is on page five of four thousand words, and page five has nine lines on it, and three of them are crossed out. Day two. His hands don’t know what they’re for. Every few minutes the right one leaves the pen and goes looking for the thing it does at a stop like this, when the doors slide open and everybody stretches and somebody says *ten minutes* and finds the pen again instead. The pack rides in the Carhartt’s breast pocket where the tin used to, square and light, sealed.

body.text: At the next table Kevin has the KEVIN Tupperware open in front of him and is eating the last of the lemon pound cake out of it with a white plastic fork, in small bites, looking out at the boulders. Sweets were his Lent, as of yesterday at Baton Rouge. He eats every bit of it anyway, slowly, down to the crumbs in the corners, and doesn’t say a word.
body.else: At the next table Kevin is peeling a gas-station banana with surgical care, a strip at a time, laying the strips out on a napkin in a fan in case anybody asks him to account for them.

body: Margot has the bench end of Jack’s table, sitting sideways, with her notebook on her knee and her collar up, reading something she wrote earlier and not liking it.

Out among the rocks, a hundred yards up the slope where the path goes between two boulders leaning together like old men at a graveside, Lena has walked Laney out of earshot. It’s a picture with the sound off. Laney has Coco under one arm; she takes her everywhere now. Lena talks. Her hands go out flat, and come together, and one of them pushes the hair out of her face and the wind puts it right back. Laney’s free hand goes up over her mouth, and the other one follows it, coconut and all, so that Coco ends up against her cheek, and she sits down on a boulder all at once, as though somebody had cut a string. She sits there. Lena stands in front of her in the wind and waits. Then Laney gets up and takes hold of her, hard, with the coconut squashed in the middle, and holds on, and keeps holding on, long enough that a family in matching Hawkeyes sweatshirts coming down the rocks with a camera has to go around them.
“Eleven minutes,” Margot says to her notebook.
“You’re timing them.”
“I’m a social scientist. Everything is a stopwatch.” She turns a page. “You’re not even pretending to write.”
He doesn’t need the sound. He knows what Lena would tell her best friend on a rock in Arizona and where she would stop: Julian, Sunday, after Mass, to his face — and nothing past the comma.

Laney comes down first, alone, walking fast against the wind with the coconut and her sunglasses pushed up on her head. Theo has been leaning in the van’s open side door with his arms folded since they stopped, and when she gets to him he unfolds them and opens his mouth.
“Don’t,” Laney says.
“I wasn’t —”
“Don’t you *dare*.”

Theo shuts his mouth. Laney turns her back on him and on the whole lot and stands at the van’s side mirror doing something to her face with the heel of her hand. Theo looks off at the boulders with his hands in his pockets. From the table Jack can see the two of them three feet apart, each carrying something filled to the brim and neither about to set it down in front of the other, and he keeps his face exactly where it is.
Kevin gets up and walks his trash over to the can by the van, and stops there, beside them, and drops it in.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, to the trash can, which is to say to both of them. “Whatever y’all aren’t saying to each other — keep not saying it.”
He walks off to the drinking fountain.
At the end of Jack’s bench Margot writes something short. She turns the notebook round on her knee so it faces him across the table.

body.title: Margot’s notebook, turned around on her knee
body.text: Field note. Subjects A and B maintain a mutual avoidance rite. Observers C and D have now adopted one toward each other. Contagion.

body: “Who’s C?” Jack says.
“Don’t be coy,” says Margot, and turns it back, and caps her pen.

Lena comes down off the rocks by herself a minute later, her hands in the jean jacket and her hair all over her face, and doesn’t come to the tables. She goes around to the far side of the van and stands there with the wind at her back and the roof of the Odyssey in front of her, like a counter she’s waiting at.

body.text: On the levee he told her that Theo and Laney threw the towel in, in Arizona, and picked it back up. This is Arizona. They’re holding it now, the pair of them, so carefully they can’t even look at it.

body: Up on the tabletop he’s high enough to see over the luggage rack, and across the roof of the van he catches her eye. She doesn’t smile. He doesn’t. It’s a near thing on both sides of the roof.

Laney has had her back to the lot long enough to put her face back where she keeps it. She turns around with the coconut in both hands and crosses the lot to Jack’s table in her Uggs, straight through the wind, and she has not once walked toward him on purpose since January. She sets Coco down on Hale’s legal pad, square on page five, fleur-de-lis up.
“Hold her,” Laney says. “With your *life*.”

response: “I’ll guard her with my life.”

“See that you do.” Laney turns on the heel of her Ugg and walks back to the van, and halfway there her sunglasses come down off the top of her head and over her eyes like a visor, and she doesn’t turn around again.

response: “Thank you, Laney.”
She’s already turned to go. She stops with her back to him, in the wind, with her arms folded. “Don’t make it weird, Jack.”
It’s the first time she’s said his name since January. She leaves it with him.

response: “Does she have a seat belt?”
“She has a *glovebox*.” And Laney is back across the lot and into the van with the side door rolled shut behind her while he’s still working out whether that was a yes.

response: He picks it up off the pad in both hands, carefully, like something that might go off. It’s lighter than it looks, and still warm from her arm.
Laney watches him hold it. She nods, as if a contract has been signed.

s13.slug: THURSDAY · 6:45 PM · BLYTHE, CALIFORNIA — THE INSPECTION STATION, AND A PUMP
body: “We gained another one.” Kevin reaches over the wheel and thumbs the dash clock back an hour, to Pacific, while the Colorado goes by underneath them in the dark, wide and black, with one light on it far downstream. “Logging it.”

The radio is off. It went off at the Broadway Curve, where Phoenix held them forty minutes in six lanes of brake lights at rush hour and Kevin reached over and stopped a traffic reporter in the middle of a sentence and said, “Atmosphere.” It has stayed stopped.

A mile into California the agricultural inspection station comes up out of the desert, a row of booths under white light, a toll plaza that wants to know how you live. A woman in a state windbreaker leans down to Kevin’s window with a flashlight. “Any fruits or vegetables?”
“Yes, ma’am,” says Kevin, who is not built for any other answer, and the bag of Plaquemines satsumas goes out of Celeste’s cooler and out the window, every one of them, still cold.
In the way-back Laney sits up. “Not *all* of them.”
“All of them,” says the inspector.
“Goodbye, Clovis,” Laney says as the bag goes. “Goodbye, Big Tony. Goodbye, the little one with the leaf.”
“You *named* them,” Theo says.
“Since Lafayette. They were very good company, Theodore, which is more than I can —”
Beside her, with her eyes shut, Lena says, “Sweet suffering Saint Sebastian.”
The flashlight goes on round the van and finds the glovebox, which Margot has open for the registration, and in the glovebox, fleur-de-lis up, Coco. “What’s that?”
Laney comes over the back of the middle seats in one movement, a knee on Theo’s armrest and Theo saying *ow*, and takes the coconut out herself and holds it up into the beam in both hands.

“Ma’am,” she says, “before you say anything, I want you to know who you’re talking to. This is Coco. Coco Chanel Price. She is a hand-painted coconut from the Zulu Social Aid and Pleasure Club, Mardi Gras morning, Jackson Avenue, and she was not *thrown*. Zulu hasn’t thrown one in twenty years, it’s a liability thing. She was *handed down*. A man on a float the size of a Piggly Wiggly leaned all the way over the rail and put her in my hands personally and looked me in the eye. She is drained. She is dried. She has been painted by an artist and blessed by a Baptist, which is me, lapsed. She has no seeds, no bugs and no agricultural *agenda*. She is not produce, ma’am. She is *heritage*. And if the State of California wants her, the State of California is going to have to go through Texas.”

The inspector takes the coconut. She hefts it in one hand and gives it a shake by her ear — nothing in it moves — and turns it over under the light, the gold and the black and the painted face grinning up at her. “It’s dried,” she says. “It’s a craft.” She hands it back through Kevin’s window. “Drive safe.”
“A *craft*,” Laney says, sitting back down with Coco in her lap, outraged and vindicated in equal parts, and Kevin pulls through into California.
At a Chevron on the east edge of Blythe, under a canopy so bright it hums, Kevin goes in to pay and Jack works the pump, and the RAZR goes off in his breast pocket against the pack. SKYE (MISFIT).

Behind him the side door is open, and Lena climbs out of the way-back with Laney and the two of them walk across the lot toward the store, Laney’s arm through hers, Lena’s hands in the jean jacket. He watches her go, once, the length of the lot under the lights. He turns around to the pump and opens the phone.
“Hi,” Skye says.
“Hi.”

And then she’s somebody else: a long-haul trucker on a CB with a sinus condition and a lot of time to think. “Breaker one-nine, this is Burnaby, B.C., looking for a Catholic. Got a report of a Catholic westbound, no smokes, sad eyes, over.”
“He’s at a pump in Blythe, California. Over.”
“Where’s Blythe. Over.”
“The first place in California. Or the last. Depends which way you’re pointed.”

“Copy that.” The trucker signs off. “I’m in the chair. They’re gluing a wound on my neck. Kyle came in with a cold and is being very brave about it in a way that’s bothering everybody. How’s the no-cigarettes? Tell me true.”
“I bought a pack of cigarettes in El Paso.”
“Did you smoke it?”
“No.”
“Why’d you buy it?”
He watches the numbers turn over on the pump. “So I’d have to not open it. Every hour.”

She laughs, short, the laugh she does when somebody on set does a thing she’s going to steal. “That’s the most Method thing I’ve ever heard. You’re going to win something.” Somebody on her end says *chin up*, and she must lift it, because her voice comes from a different angle.

“Okay. Listen. Tuesday. I land at LAX at twelve-ten, and I drive up, and I’ll be a mess of a person on the 101 for two hours, it’ll be good for me. Del Playa. Six. I’ll leave the porch light on.” He can hear her smiling. “Don’t eat. I’m making you dinner. I’ve never made anybody dinner. Wear something you can get eggs on.”
“What are you making?”
“Eggs. Some kind of eggs. I’ve watched a man at craft services do it on a griddle about four thousand times; I think I’ve absorbed it. It’s a frittata. It’s eggs with ambition.”
The pump clicks off. He hangs the nozzle back in its cradle.
“Okay,” he says.
“Is Ted there? Put Ted on.”

Theo is coming back across the lot from the store with two bottles of water. Jack holds the phone out. Theo stops a yard off and looks at it in Jack’s hand. He moves both waters into one hand and takes it.

“Callender,” he says. “It’s going beautifully. We’re ahead of schedule, Kevin has a margin note. The beignets Tuesday morning came in at sixty-two grams apiece — I asked the girl at the counter to weigh one, and she did, and she was moved. I had nine. Rex had twenty-eight floats. I counted. Kevin says twenty-seven; Kevin missed the one with the duck. We have a coconut in the van with a longer provenance than mine, which as of half an hour ago has been determined by the State of California to be a *craft*, and she’s taking it personally. The boy is fine. The boy is a model citizen. He has the moral fiber of a Shaker chair.” He listens. “Break a leg. Figuratively. I’ve read the cast insurance.”

He hands the RAZR back without looking at Jack and walks off with the two waters to the far end of the lot, past the air hose and the ice chest, to where the canopy light gives out at the edge of the desert, and stands there with his back to the Chevron.

“Hi again,” Skye says. She has the phone closer; her mouth is right against it, low, under the noise of whatever room she’s in. “I keep thinking about your forehead. The ashes. Where they were.” A breath. “Tuesday I’m going to find the place. And then I’m going to find it with my mouth.”
He puts his forehead against the steel of the pump, right where the ash was. The steel is cold.
“I miss you so much it’s embarrassing,” she says. “Don’t tell the goose.” Somebody says her name on her end, and a door, and she says *one minute* away from the phone, and comes back to it. “Five.”

choices.key: At a gas pump in Blythe Skye told you she’d leave the porch light on Tuesday and make you dinner. You told her you love her.
response: “Love you,” he says.
“Love you. Bye, Pack.”
He stands at the pump with the phone shut in his hand and the cold of the steel still on his forehead.

choices.text: “Tuesday. I’ll tell you all of it. To your face.”
choices.key: At a gas pump in Blythe Skye told you she’d leave the porch light on Tuesday and make you dinner. You told her you’d tell her all of it Tuesday, to her face.
response: “Tuesday,” he says. “I’ll tell you all of it. To your face.”
“You’d better. Every float. Every bead. I want the parade in order, with the weather.” The door again, on her end. “Bye, Pack.” And the line goes.

choices.key: At a gas pump in Blythe Skye told you she’d leave the porch light on Tuesday and make you dinner. You told her not to burn the house down.
response: “Don’t burn Del Playa down.”

“No promises. There’s a fire extinguisher. I’ve never looked at it, but I believe in it. Bye, Pack.” She’s laughing when the line goes, and he stands under the humming canopy with the RAZR shut in his hand and the sound of it still in his ear.

s13a.slug: THURSDAY · 7:05 PM · BLYTHE — FOR YOUR HANDS
body: Lena and Laney come back across the lot with a plastic bag swinging between them, and Lena climbs in first, over the middle row and into the way-back, and puts her face to the far window.
When Jack gets back to his chair there is something on it.

A bag of sunflower seeds, in the shell, the big salted kind the old men used to spit all over the lot outside the Lordstown gate while they waited on the shift whistle. Across the front of it, over the brand, in black marker, in her block capitals: FOR YOUR HANDS.

He doesn’t turn around. If he turns around he’ll have to have a face, and he doesn’t own one he’s allowed to use in this van. He sits down with the bag on his knee. In the next chair Theo looks at the bag, and at the writing on it, and then out his own window for a long time at a Chevron sign.

Indio, the date palms black against what’s left of the west. Over the pass the windmills, a thousand of them in the dark and nothing of them but the red lights on top, blinking in long rows all together, and under the blinking at Cabazon the dinosaurs, a brontosaurus and a tyrannosaur, two black shapes standing over a gift shop that closed hours ago. The 10 down into Los Angeles at half past ten, the basin lit to its edges. The 101. Ventura. The Rincon, where he watched the sun come up two weeks ago going the other way. He opens the bag at Indio, and he cracks the seeds one at a time in his teeth — the shell, the salt, the small gray seed — and drops the shells into an empty coffee cup between his boots, and his hands have something to do, and they do it for two hundred miles.

s14.slug: FRIDAY · 12:30 AM · THE ANACAPA LOT, UNDER THE BELL TOWER — WHERE THE WATER WAS
body: The fog is in when they get there. It has come up off the Channel and over the bluff and into the Anacapa lot, and the lamps stand in it with rings around them, and the bell tower is a dark shape going up into nothing. It’s the coast’s kind of cold, wet, the kind that gets into the knuckles. Kevin puts the van into the same space it left from.

body.text: At the end of the row, under the eucalyptus, the Saab’s space is empty. Two weeks ago at a quarter to five in the morning she stood in it with her hood back, and Father Osei wet his thumb and put the water in her hair, and she shut her eyes.
body.else: At the end of the row, under the eucalyptus, the Saab’s space is empty. Two weeks ago she stood in it in the dark with her hood up and waved until they were out of the lot.

body: Kevin turns the engine off. In the tick of it cooling he takes the sheet down off the dash, clicks his pen and writes the time in the last box, and reads it out to the van.

“Thirty-five fifteen.” He looks at it. “Twenty-five minutes faster than the way down.” He folds the sheet in quarters along the creases he made in Mid-City. “Nobody fought.” And he puts it in his wallet, behind his license.

Six people unfold themselves into the fog. Laney’s quilted bags come out of the hatch one after another, a matched set, and Coco comes out of the glovebox in her arms. Theo carries two bags up the walk that aren’t his and doesn’t notice. Margot comes last, with the motel’s Gideon back under her arm like a library book she has every intention of returning. Under the lot light, on the back glass, WHO DAT · 40 DAYS has gone streaky in the wet. Jack takes Celeste’s cooler off Kevin without asking, with nothing left in it but Gloria’s tin, and Kevin lets go of it, and claps him on the shoulder, and says nothing about hazards to navigation.
“We’re home, baby,” Laney tells the coconut. “Don’t look at the weather.”
“And scene,” says Theo, from halfway up the walk.

Lena is the last one out of the way-back. She stands by the van a minute with her duffel strap over her shoulder, looking up at the bell tower where it goes into the white. There are two days of van on her face, the same as on his, and the fog is beading on the wool of her collar as it beads on everybody’s here, and it’s the first time he has seen it bead on hers in two weeks. Then she comes up the walk, and he comes up the walk, with the cooler, on the other side of it, and the fog goes up the walk with them, and nobody has to explain anything to anybody. Through the glass of the Delgado door the night desk is empty, and somebody has taped a sign inside it, laminated, QUIET HOURS ARE A KINDNESS, which has Priya written all over it.
At the door Lena turns around.
“It’s Friday,” she says.

body.text: “Bread and water.”
body.else: “Bread and water,” he says. He means hers, the docket she read out to the van at Baton Rouge. He never told her it was his too.

body.text: “Nobody asked you,” she says, so gently it hardly counts, and goes up the stairs with her duffel knocking her knee.
body.else: She’s up the first flight with her duffel knocking her knee before he can tell her.

body: From the landing, over the rail, with the stairwell light on her hair: “Goodnight, Jack.”
He stands in the doorway with the cooler on his hip and the fog coming in around his boots until he hears her door shut somewhere above him.

s15.slug: FRIDAY · 6:45 AM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — HOME
body: He wakes at twenty to seven, and for a second he doesn’t know the ceiling. It’s his. The window is gray with the Pacific past the roofs, and the eucalyptus outside is doing what it does in the wet, and on the wall over his bed the crucifix is where he hung it in August.
Theo is awake in the other bed, on his back with one arm behind his head, looking at the ceiling.
“How long have you been up?”
“Define *up*.”
Jack’s hands are awake before the rest of him. He finds them at the drawstring of the duffel at the foot of the bed, working the knot in and out, and he takes them back and tucks them under his arms.
“You talk in your sleep,” Theo says. “You said ‘Atchafalaya.’ Twice. With longing. I nearly called someone.”
“Who?”

“A priest. A Cajun. Whoever handles that.” Theo turns his head on the pillow and looks across the room at him — at the duffel still packed at the foot of the bed, at the man sitting up in a T-shirt with his hands in his armpits. “Welcome home, Father Jack.”

On the desk by the bed is two weeks of mail he carried up from the front desk at one in the morning and dropped there without looking at it, and on top of it everything out of his pockets: the RAZR, his wallet, the sunflower seeds with a third of the bag left, and the pack, red and white, the cellophane catching the window, a reach away from the foot of the crucifix. Most of the mail is the bursar and a flyer for a Lenten soup supper at St. Brendan’s. One envelope is in Gina’s handwriting from Glenwood Avenue, and inside it is a purple card with a cross on the front, and on the back, in pencil, the letters leaning on one another, Nonna’s English:

body.title: A Lenten card from Glenwood Avenue — Gina’s handwriting on the envelope, Nonna’s inside
body.text:
Giacomino —
Quaresima. I give up the coffee. Your mother says pray for her, so pray for her.
Bring Maria Caterina this summer so I can see is she too thin.
Nonna

body: He reads it sitting on the edge of the bed with his bare feet on the cold floor, and then he sets it face down on the desk.

body.text: Mémère’s St. Joseph card is propped on the headboard ledge under the crucifix, where he stood it at one in the morning without deciding to: St. Joseph with his lily and his carpenter’s square, looking off to one side, in no hurry.
body.else: Tony’s card for Gloria is in the wallet on the desk, behind his license, where it has been since the walk-in.

body: At ten to seven he calls his mother. She’s at her desk in the office at St. Brigid’s, and she picks up on the first ring.
“There he is.”
“I’m back, Ma. Got in at one.”
“How long in that car?”
“Thirty-five hours.”
Ma doesn’t say anything right away. In January she didn’t either. “That isn’t tired,” she says. “I know tired.”
“I’ll sleep, Ma.”
“Did you eat?”
“It’s Friday.”
“That’s not an answer, that’s a calendar.” Somebody comes into her office for the copier key, and he listens to her find it. “Your grandmother sent you a card.”
“I’ve got it.”
“Then you know,” Ma says, and has to go.

He kneels at the window on the floor between the beds, as he has knelt on deck boards and motel carpet and the ribbed floor of a van, and starts. *He summoned the Twelve and began to send them out two by two —*
And stops. *Every morning until you are home.* The window is full of Marisol: wet roofs, the eucalyptus, the gray lifting off the water a little at a time. He’s home.

choices.text: *Say it anyway, all the way to the oil.*
response: He goes on. Fifteen mornings. The walking stick, the sandals, the dust off the feet, and the last verse — *they anointed with oil many who were sick, and cured them* — and he stays on his knees a minute after it with nothing left to say.

When he gets up he takes the pack off the desk and puts it back in the Carhartt’s breast pocket, and his stomach turns over once, empty, like an engine in January that won’t catch. Bread and water. He does up the button.

choices.text: *Stop. You’re home. Say a Hail Mary for Skye instead.*
response: He says a Hail Mary for Skye. He gets as far as *now and at the hour* and has to stop there a minute, on his knees between the beds, before he can finish it.

The pack is where he left it on the desk, red and white and sealed, a reach from the crucifix. He looks at it. Then he puts it in the Carhartt anyway, and his stomach, which has worked out what day it is, says so out loud, and Theo says, “Amen.”
He gets up.
“People don’t just *get up*, Costigan,” Theo says from the bed. “It’s unnatural. There should be a swell of strings.”

Jack picks the pack up off the desk and drops it into the Carhartt’s breast pocket and buttons the flap down, and stands there in his socks with his stomach hollow as a bell, because it’s Friday, and the morning hasn’t even started.

s16.slug: FRIDAY · 12:20 PM · ANACAPA COMMONS — BREAD AND WATER
body: Day three of the habit told no, the first Friday of Lent, maybe five hours of sleep in the last forty-eight, and Jack Costigan is the crankiest man in California. He knows it. He can feel it on him like a sunburn: the itch under the skin of his forearms, the fog behind his eyes, a fuse burning short. On his tray there is a roll, a glass of water, and a pat of butter he took off the stack by reflex and is now in a standoff with.

The Commons at noon on a Friday is a din. Trays, the soft-serve machine grinding, a birthday at the long table, and the TV over the salad bar, muted, where a man in a dark suit stands at a podium in a blue room and reads to a roomful of people from sheets of paper, and Jack thinks of Remy’s poster hanging upside down by one tack in an attic on Dupre Street, the fist still up.
Across from him Theo is eating a cheeseburger. He eats it slowly and in full view, turning it after every bite to choose the next one.
“Eat it faster,” Jack says.
“I’m savoring.” Theo touches a napkin to the corner of his mouth. “I’m not Catholic, Costigan. I’m *supportive*.”

Jack’s right hand has torn the crust off the roll in small pieces and built them into a pile, and is now taking the pile apart. Kevin, beside Theo with a tuna sandwich, watches the hand with professional interest, and then reaches over and moves Jack’s plastic knife out of range.
“Hypoglycemic and withdrawing,” Kevin says. “You shouldn’t operate a stapler.”

Behind Jack a guy at the next table shoves his chair back, and the metal feet shriek on the tile, and Jack turns clear around in his seat and looks at him. The guy, who is enormous and wearing a lacrosse pinny, says, “Sorry, man. Sorry,” and sits back down very gently.
“That was a look,” Theo says, impressed. “Save it for Hale on Monday.”
“Stations are at seven,” Kevin says. “I’m saving the second pew.”
“Save it for somebody else.”
“I always do,” says Kevin, sunny, and eats his sandwich.
Margot is at the end of the table with a bowl of soup, reading.
Becca Lindell comes by with a tray, a fish sandwich in its paper boat, and slows at their table and smiles at him, as she smiles at everybody coming out of the eleven-thirty. “First Friday.”
“First Friday,” Jack says, and she goes on toward the Newman table by the doors.

At the window table across the room, the good one, with the Pacific behind it, Lena is sitting with Laney, and on Lena’s tray there is a roll and a glass of water. Laney, whose Lent lasted until Phoenix, has a basket of curly fries on the table and is eating them at Lena one at a time, like a dare, talking with her hands. Lena tears off a corner of the roll and eats it, and drinks some water, and listens to whatever it is with her chin up, a girl at a dinner party being very polite to a soup.

body.text: She looks across the room the way you check a clock, and sees his tray. Something happens at the corner of her mouth, small, and is put away again.
body.else: She looks over and sees his tray. She looks at it a long time — the roll, the water, nothing else — and then she looks at him across the din, and he can see her get it: every Friday, the same as hers.

body: Laney’s eyes go from Lena’s tray to Jack’s across the room and back to Lena’s. She puts down her fork. She gets up, takes her bag off the back of her chair, and walks out of the Commons, fast, without a word to anybody, like a person leaving a movie during the part she can’t watch.
Theo puts down the last of the cheeseburger. “Napkins,” he says, and gets up, and follows her out. There’s a stack of napkins at his elbow.
Margot doesn’t look up from her soup. “Two people eating bread and water thirty feet apart,” she says. “I’ve seen less ritual at a High Mass.”

Under the table Jack’s knee is going like a sewing machine. He could cross the room in six seconds without spilling the water; he has crossed bigger rooms than this for worse reasons, a party on Del Playa, a lounge at two in the morning. He stays in the plastic chair with both hands around the tumbler, and the six seconds go by, and go by again.

Over at the window table Lena is alone now, with Laney’s abandoned tray across from her and the fog behind her starting to burn off the water in patches. She picks up her water glass and lifts it an inch off the table, toward him, and holds it there.

choices.text: *Lift your glass back, and hold it there.*
response: He lifts his back, the scratched plastic Commons tumbler with the last of his water in it, and holds it there.
Thirty feet of trays and backpacks and somebody’s birthday go on around the two glasses, and neither comes down. Hers goes first, finally, a good deal later than she meant it to.

choices.text: *Raise the roll instead, like a toast.*
response: He raises the roll instead, what’s left of it after his hand got done with the crust, up high, a best man at a wedding.
Across the room Lena puts her face in her hand.
“Oh,” says Margot, into her soup, “that’s going in the notes.” The notebook stays in her bag.
He keeps his eyes on his tray and eats. The roll goes in eleven bites, dry, with water between, and the butter stays in its foil.
At the last bite he looks up anyway. She’s already looking somewhere else — out the window, at the water — carefully.

s17.slug: FRIDAY · 7:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE STATIONS
body: St. Brendan’s keeps its lights low for the Stations: the sanctuary lamp, the two banks over the side aisles, and the rest of the church given back to the evening going violet in the high windows. The purple is everywhere else. It’s on the cloth at Mary’s feet where the flowers used to be, on the ambo, on the stole around Father Osei’s neck as he comes out of the sacristy behind the cross. Maybe forty people. On a Sunday night the place takes four hundred standing, and the forty have spread themselves through it with the Catholic instinct for the back half.

Joey Abruzzo has the cross. It’s the brass processional cross on its pole, a head taller than he is, and he carries it in both fists with his elbows out, and when he grounds it at the first station the knock goes up into the rafters and comes back down, and a woman in the middle pews jumps. He is too loud even holding a cross. Two acolytes from the nine o’clock come behind him with candles, the flames laid back by the walking.

The stations go round the walls, seven to a side, dark carved wood, the figures rubbed pale at the knees and knuckles by people touching them on the way past for longer than anybody here has been alive. At each one Father Osei names it and says, “We adore you, O Christ, and we praise you,” and the church answers, “Because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world,” and Mrs. Fitch, three pews from the front in her good camel coat, is always a half-step ahead of everybody else, so the answer arrives twice, hers and then theirs, an echo that got there first.

Between the stations, while the little procession turns from one wall toward the next, Gus Ferreira at the organ gives a note with only the soft stops out, and he and five or six voices up front sing a verse of the Stabat Mater in the old English, *At the cross her station keeping*, Gus’s foghorn underneath holding the rest of them up.

Jack came by himself. He walked up the hill from Delgado at a quarter to seven, and he stands at the back by the holy water, near enough the door to feel the cold come in under it. Lena is up front on the aisle in the second pew, the one Kevin said he’d save, with Kevin beside her in his windbreaker. At every station, when Father Osei says the words, she genuflects all the way to the floor, right knee down hard on the tile, and comes back up without a hand on the pew. He sees every one from the back of the church. He tells himself he’s watching the cross.

Day three, and the first day of bread and water, and he has had a roll and a half since he woke. Around four o’clock the hunger stopped being in his stomach. Now it’s in his head, a high, thin, ringing clearness, the floor a little farther down than it ought to be and the candle flames a little too sharp at the edges. His hands are the worst of it. They want the breast pocket, where the pack lies flat, and he keeps them out of it, fists in the side pockets of the Carhartt with the lining balled up inside them.

The third station, the first fall. The fourth, his mother. The fifth, Simon of Cyrene, pulled out of the crowd and made to carry it. At each one the church turns from one wall to the next with a noise of shoes and kneelers, and the cross goes ahead.

At the sixth they come to the wall nearest the door, and Joey grounds the cross not six feet from him. *Veronica wipes the face of Jesus.* In the carving she holds the cloth up in both hands, and the face is on it, small and cut deep, the only face on that wall looking straight out. Father Osei reads the meditation from the booklet and Jack doesn’t hear a word of it. On Wednesday an old man pressed ashes onto Jack’s forehead, crooked, and on Thursday the last of them went down a steel sink in Fort Stockton. *Wash your face, so that you may not appear to be fasting.* He did what it said. He looks at the cloth in the woman’s hands.
*I haven’t got a cloth,* he prays, which is as far as it gets. *Take the hands.*

At the twelfth station the church goes down on its knees on the bare floor and stays down. Jack kneels on the stone by the door with his fists still in his pockets. Up front, past all the bowed heads, he can see the back of hers, the dark of her hair against the collar of the jean jacket, and that is all he looks at until Father Osei says the words and everybody gets up.

After the fourteenth there is a last prayer and a last verse, and the lights come up a notch, and people start finding their coats and their car keys. Father Osei hands the cross off to the sacristan and comes down the side aisle still in the stole, a little uneven on the left leg, nodding to people as he goes, and he stops at the back by the holy water in front of Jack and looks at him. He takes his time. He looks at Jack’s face, and the color in it, and his eyes, and the two fists in the pockets of the Carhartt, and comes back to the face.
“You look like a man who has driven two thousand miles on no food.”
“Two thousand and six.”
Osei doesn’t smile, quite. “Saturday I hear confessions,” he says. “Three-thirty. Or whenever you knock.” And he goes back up the aisle to see about the candles.

Outside it’s full dark and the cold is coming up the hill off the Channel. Jack stands on the top step. People come out around him in twos and threes and go down to the street. Lena comes out with Kevin a step behind her sorting his keys, and she goes down past Jack, neither slow nor fast, her hands in the pockets of the jean jacket, toward Kevin’s van at the curb.
“One down,” she says, going by, and doesn’t stop.

s17a.slug: SATURDAY · 1:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — CAN’T
body: The clock on Theo’s side says 1:40. Jack has been on his back on top of his made bed since half past ten, boots off, the Carhartt still on, his hands folded on his stomach where he can see them by the light from the parking lot.

Across the room Theo is breathing slow and even, and every so often the evenness stops, and starts again a little too carefully. It isn’t sleep. Jack doesn’t say anything to it, and it doesn’t say anything to him.

The RAZR lies shut on the desk. The pack is on the desk too, under the crucifix, where he put it at midnight so his thumbnail would quit working at the tab on the cellophane: red and white, sealed, the lot light lying along it.

He has been doing the arithmetic of Tuesday for three hours. What he says first, and where: on the porch, or inside, or after she’s put the plate down. Eggs with ambition. Which chair she puts him in. Whether he lets her feed him first, and how long he can let it run before the letting is its own kind of lie. He gets to the bottom of it and starts again at the top, and it comes out the same every time, and the number won’t get any smaller.
At ten to two he sits up and puts his boots on.

choices.text: *Take the pack to the east stairwell.*

s18p.slug: SATURDAY · 2:05 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE — HER PORCH
body: He goes down Ocean Road with his hands in his pockets and the cold coming through the denim at the knees. At Las Olas a party is going out like a tide: a front door standing open on a hallway of red cups, three boys on the curb sharing the last of a pizza out of the box, a couch dragged onto the lawn with a girl asleep on it under somebody’s letterman jacket, and up on a second-floor balcony another girl singing the chorus of “TiK ToK” down at the parked cars, the same part over and over, with total sincerity. The jasmine on the fences isn’t out yet. Past it Del Playa goes quiet, the ocean-side houses dark against a sky without a star in it, and under their back decks the surf comes in and pulls out.

Her house is dark. He knew it would be; she’s in Burnaby in a makeup chair with somebody gluing a wound onto her neck. The porch still leans a little to the left, toward the neighbors, and the swing hangs at the far end on its chains, and he doesn’t sit in the swing. He sits on her top step. Over the door the porch light is off. Tuesday she’ll leave it on.

By the door her rain boots stand side by side, yellow, the left one with a script rolled up and pushed down inside it to the brads so the wind won’t have it. On the rail there’s a coffee can of beach glass, mostly green and brown, with one blue piece balanced on the top that she must have found last and liked best, because that’s where she put it. He nearly laughs at the boots. Of course she’d keep a script in a boot. She’d keep it where she has to put her foot in it in the morning and remember she has lines.

If he leans out past the post he can see the turnout down the road, the dark scoop of gravel past the Marine Lab fence where the Saab used to sit with the engine off and the heater on and the two of them in it, talking, till the windows went white.

This is where he’ll tell her. On this porch, under that light, in three days, with her standing about where the boots are. He makes himself look at it: the door, the boards, the place she’ll stand. He hasn’t got the first sentence. He has her face when it gets there, and he can’t look at that, so he looks at the blue glass.
The pack is in his breast pocket the entire time, and sitting on her steps with the ocean going in and out under the house, he doesn’t think about it at all. He notices that, and wishes he hadn’t.
The RAZR goes against it. SKYE (MISFIT), on her meal break.

s18s.slug: SATURDAY · 2:05 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — NO. 13
body: The push bar is cold under his hand. The east stairwell hasn’t changed: cinderblock painted a cream gone yellow, the steel rail, the fluorescent tube over the landing humming its one note, and the cold that lives in here all year whatever the rest of Delgado is doing. He sits on the third step down from the fourth floor. In January he smoked one on this step at twenty to four in the morning, and nine days after that he sat on it with one in his fingers and put it back.

Up here, past two, the building has gone as quiet as it gets. Somebody’s music comes up the well from a long way down, a bass line and nothing else, and somewhere a toilet runs and runs. The wired-glass window on the landing is black, with his own reflection in it sitting on a step in a Carhartt, which he doesn’t look at long.
He takes the pack out of the breast pocket and turns it end over end on his knee, Kevin’s trick with his BlackBerry. Red and white. The cellophane takes the tube light and gives it back.

It’s the worst hour of the third day and he can feel all of it: the itch along the insides of his forearms that scratching can’t get to, the hollow of a day of bread and water, the fog behind his eyes from three nights of next to nothing, and under all of that the want. His thumbnail finds the tab on the cellophane. He gets the nail under it.

He doesn’t pull it. He doesn’t take the nail out either. He sits there with it under the tab and says the St. Michael prayer under his breath, all of it, as it’s printed on the card in his wallet, *defend us in battle, be our protection against the wickedness and snares of the devil*, and it doesn’t make the want go anywhere. It gives his mouth something to do. He says it again.
Three days from now he’ll be on a porch on Del Playa with a woman who is going to make him eggs. He thinks about her laughing at the pack in Blythe, and keeps the nail where it is.
*Whatever you’re doing, Jack — you can stop.*

The tube hums. Somewhere below, a door on the second floor opens and shuts, and somebody laughs in the hall and is gone. He sits with the nail under the tab until his thumb aches, and takes it out, and puts the pack back in the breast pocket, and does up the button.
The RAZR goes against it. SKYE (MISFIT), on her meal break.
