s19.slug: SATURDAY · 6:55 AM → 1:00 PM · THE ANCHOR — THE FISHERMEN

body.text: *Come back the twentieth and earn them.* It’s the twentieth. The window over the Channel went gray at six without his having slept, and he stood under the shower on four till the hot ran out. He comes in the Anchor’s back door at five to seven with Gloria’s tin under his arm and his hair still wet, and the kitchen is the kitchen: the Hobart breathing steam, the radio on the shelf over the line playing something low in Spanish, Rudy at the sink with his sleeves pushed up and his rosary on the shelf above it where it lives. The fishermen shift is still his.
body.else: He gave Hector the Saturdays from a front step in New Orleans. The window over the Channel went gray at six without his having slept, and he stood under the shower on four till the hot ran out, and he comes anyway, at five to seven, in the front door with the customers, with Gloria’s tin under his arm and his hair still wet. Through the pass he can see Hector on the Hobart. Gloria looks at him over the case, and at the tin, and points the grease pencil at a stool. “You gave him your Saturdays. Sit.”

body: Gloria is behind the case with the grease pencil pushed through the knot of her hair, giving the pies their quarter-turn, one and then the next, so the good side faces the door. From seven on the bell over the door goes every couple of minutes, and she doesn’t look up for it. She never has.

body.text: The fishermen shift runs seven to one: men off the boats in the harbor with salt in the seams of their hands, who pay in cash and tip in it and want their eggs before they’ve finished sitting down. Merle has his chowder at eight in the morning, as he does, and swears it’s a breakfast food in Gloucester. Jack takes the pit. Day four, no sleep, and the dish pit is a mercy. The racks come and the racks go, the spray arm bangs, the steam comes up into his face, and his hands have a job. They’re too busy to want anything. Rudy, rinsing beside him, watches the speed of him and says, soft, “Mijo. The plates aren’t going anywhere,” and goes back to his pots.
body.else: So he sits. The fishermen come in off the boats at seven with salt in the seams of their hands, paying in cash, and Merle has his chowder at eight in the morning, as he does, and swears it’s a breakfast food in Gloucester, and Hector runs the Hobart faster than Jack ever ran it. Jack sits at the end of the counter with a coffee and nothing for his hands and the pack in his pocket, until a little after nine, when Gloria sets a bus tub of clean silverware and a brick of paper napkins in front of him and walks off. He rolls silverware till one. It’s a mercy. His hands have a job.

body.text: In the lull at ten he sets the tin on the counter by the register — the pie tin with the boysenberry ghost still in the corner — and takes the lid off. Mémère’s pralines, stacked in their squares of wax paper, the pecans gone glassy at the edges. “Lena’s grandmother made them,” he says. “Her mother says a tin goes back full. She says it’s not manners, it’s law.”

Mémère’s pralines, stacked in their squares of wax paper, the pecans gone glassy at the edges. “Lena’s grandmother made them,” he says. “Her mother says a tin goes back full. She says it’s not manners, it’s law.”

body: Gloria takes one. She eats it standing, with her eyes on the case, and chews, and swallows, and wipes her thumb on her apron.
“Nine,” she says. And to the case, not to him: “Thirty years. I never said nine out loud.”
She puts the lid back on the tin and puts the tin under the counter, down by her purse, where nobody on the line is going to get at it.
Around eleven Merle leans in at the pass with his empty bowl and looks at Jack through the steam. “You get any beads down there?”
“A few.”
“You look like you got run over by the parade, kid.” He sets the bowl in the window.

body.text: He gets Tony’s card out of his wallet from behind his license and puts it on the counter where the tin was. She reads the back, FOR GLORIA in carpenter’s pencil, and turns it over and reads the front, and turns it back. “Tell him I don’t fly,” she says, and puts it in her apron pocket, and it doesn’t come out again.

body: At one the Hobart shuts down with a long sigh, and Rudy hangs his apron on its nail and takes his rosary down off the shelf and puts it in his shirt pocket, and the last of the fishermen counts out his ones on the counter and goes. When the room is empty she puts a slice of the Dutch apple in front of him at the counter with a fork stuck upright in it. It’s Saturday. Nothing stands between him and a slice of pie but himself.
“Eat.” She looks at his face as she looks at a pie through the case glass, to see if it’s set. “You look like a man with somewhere to be.”

response: “Don’t thank me. Come back.” She goes off down the counter with the pot.
He eats every bite, down to the crust at the point, which he has never in his life eaten.

choices.text: “Thank you for letting me come anyway.”
response: “Don’t thank me. Eat.”
He eats. He eats it to the last flake on the plate, and she takes the plate away with the fork still on it.
“Mémère can come say it.” She puts a second slice down next to the first.
He eats both. It takes him until a quarter to two, and Rudy, going out the back with his jacket on, stops to watch him finish the second one, and nods.
“Then you eat the whole slice.”

She stands there till he does, the grease pencil in her hair and her arms folded, and when he puts the fork down on the clean plate she looks at the plate and then at him. “Seven,” she says, and it isn’t clear which of them she means.

s20.slug: SATURDAY · 3:30 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — THE LINE
body: The late sun comes in gold through the west windows and lies across the pews in long bars, and the dust turns over slowly in it. The Saturday line in Lent is longer than the Saturday line any other time: students down the side aisle in sweatshirts and flip-flops, two old women with their own kneelers’ worth of patience, a man in a Cal Poly jacket with his hands clasped in front of him, a girl reading an examination of conscience off a folded pamphlet and moving her lips. Out in the vestibule Mrs. Fitch is at the desk counting the week’s envelopes in a whisper.

Over the confessional door the little light is on. Under it the card says KNOCK (GENTLY), and under that (AND PROMPTLY), in Father Osei’s hand, and nothing else now; there’s a strip of cleaner card at the bottom where the tape was.

Lena is in the line ahead of him, four people between them: the two old women, the Cal Poly jacket, the girl with the pamphlet. She’s in the jean jacket, and he can see the square of the tin in its chest pocket from here. She doesn’t turn around. Day four, and he has had Gloria’s pie and no sleep, and he is steadier than he was yesterday and has no skin at all, and he kneels in the back pew and keeps his eyes on the light.
At twenty to four she turns around. She looks at him down the length of the aisle, one look, straight, and turns back.
The door opens and somebody comes out, and she goes in.

Later she comes out. She goes to the side pew by the Marian shrine and kneels there for her penance with her head down, and then she gets up and leaves by the side door, and the side door is behind the back pew, behind him. He hears her go by. He doesn’t turn.

The old women go in, one and then the other. The Cal Poly jacket goes in. The girl with the pamphlet folds it up small and goes in. When it’s his turn Jack stays on his knees and lets the man who came in behind him go first, and the next, a boy with a skateboard under his arm, and a woman in scrubs, and a couple who go in one after the other while the one waiting holds the other’s coat. He lets every one of them go. The bars of sun move up off the pews and onto the wall.
When the last of them has gone out the front, he’s the only one left in the church. Over the choir loft the clock says 4:14. The light over the door stays on.

s21.slug: SATURDAY · 4:15 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, FATHER OSEI’S OFFICE — TWO CHAIRS
s21.music: Nana Ampadu & the African Brothers Band — “Ebi Te Yie”
body: At a quarter past, the confessional door opens and Father Osei puts his head out and looks down the empty aisle at the one man left in the back pew. He looks a good while, at how Jack is kneeling and the color of him and what his hands are doing, and then he says, “Come.”

Not the box. He takes Jack up the side aisle and through the sacristy and down the hall beyond it to his office, where he sets the needle down on a record as they come in, two guitars chasing each other round and round in a high bright knot, and lets it go while he crosses the room, and lifts it again before he sits, and the room is quiet. Rubber boots by the door with the mud dried pale on them. Books on the floor in towers. On the desk a box of tissues, which lives there for exactly this. In front of the desk two wooden chairs stand side by side, both turned to the crucifix on the wall.
Father Osei takes the purple stole off the back of his desk chair. “In case,” he says, and kisses it and puts it on, and sits down in one of the two chairs, and looks at the crucifix, not at Jack.
Jack sits in the other one. Up close the office smells of the coffee in the pot on the filing cabinet, gone to tar since noon, and of rubber from the boots. His knee is going. He puts his hand on it.
“When did you sleep?” Osei asks. He is still looking at the crucifix.
“I’m good, Father.”
“You say ‘good’ the way my patients said ‘fine,’” says Father Osei. “Well. We will come back to it.”
“Bless me, Father —”

And there’s nothing after it. *It has been* — he knows the next words, he has said them since he was seven — but nothing that goes after them belongs there yet, and he sits with his mouth open on it, and his hands come up off his knees and go back down.
“Then don’t,” Osei says. “Tell me what happened. We will see what it is after.”

He tells him. It comes out in the wrong order, end first. “We’re both — by the end of the week. Both of us. She’s ending it Sunday. Tomorrow. After Mass, to his face. And I’m telling Skye Tuesday, when she lands. To her face.” He has to stop and go back. “On the levee. In New Orleans, the night before Ash Wednesday. We nearly — and we both stopped. The same second. And then we talked till nearly midnight. Everything since October. All of it. And we said nothing till then. Nothing either one of us would have to explain.” He looks at his hands. “So we haven’t.”

He stops because he has run out of air. He has been talking fast and high and getting nowhere, and his hands are shaking on his knees from no sleep and no cigarettes and the bread and water of yesterday, and his eyes are stinging, and he tells himself that’s the no sleep too. The tissues are right there. He doesn’t take one. Father Osei doesn’t offer.

body.text: “Tuesday,” he says. “To her face. I promised her that. In a darkroom. Before I left.”
body.else: “Tuesday,” he says. “To her face. That’s the least she gets.”

body: Osei looks at the crucifix. His hands are folded on his stomach, the wooden rosary on his belt under them. “And what is it you want me to do with that?”
“Nothing,” Jack says. “I’m not asking you if I can, Father. I know. I knew on the levee.”
“All right.”
The radiator ticks. Jack sits there. He knows. That isn’t it, and he can’t get to what it is, and his right hand has found the hem of the Carhartt and is twisting it.
“It’s Skye,” he says. “I love her.”
“I know,” says Father Osei. “I have heard you say so, in that box.”

body.text: “On the levee I started to say what she is to me,” he says. “And I stopped.”
“I told Lena I’d tell Skye all of it, to her face. And I will. And I love her.”
“On the levee I stopped, and let it be quiet. That was the most honest thing I said all night.”
“Mary Catherine,” he says. He has said it out loud maybe four times in his life. “That’s her name. Her real one.”
body.else: “Skye,” he says again, to the crucifix, as though the name might do some of it for him.

body: And then the thing under it.

choices.text: “I was going to marry her someday, Father. Not soon. Someday. I had the chair picked out at my grandmother’s table.”
choices.key: In Father Osei’s office you told him you’d planned to marry Skye someday — you had the chair picked out at your grandmother’s table.
response: “I was going to marry her someday, Father. Not soon. Someday. I had the chair picked out at my grandmother’s table.”

The chair by the radiator at the kitchen table on Glenwood, Nonna’s corner, where she can reach over and fix your collar while you eat. He’d had Skye in it since Christmas. And then Gina’s text, at one in the morning, back in January, and he says it word for word, because he knows it word for word: “*Nonna says Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife.*”

response.text: “I told Skye she said it. She heard it.”

choices.text: “My grandmother said Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife. I told Skye she said it. I meant it.”
choices.key: In Father Osei’s office you told him what your grandmother said — Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife — and that you’d told Skye, and meant it.
response: “My grandmother said Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife. I told Skye she said it. I meant it.”

And the rest, because it’s there behind it: not soon. Someday. He’d had a chair for her at the kitchen table on Glenwood, the one by the radiator in Nonna’s corner. He’d had her in it since Christmas.

choices.text: “My grandmother said Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife. I never told Skye. I meant it anyway.”
choices.key: In Father Osei’s office you told him what your grandmother said — Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife — and that you’d meant it.
response: “My grandmother said Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife. I never told Skye. I meant it anyway.”
And the rest, because it’s there behind it: not soon. Someday. A chair at the kitchen table on Glenwood, the one by the radiator in Nonna’s corner.

choices.text: *Say nothing for a while. Let him wait.*
choices.key: In Father Osei’s office you sat a long time without saying anything. Then you told him you’d meant to marry her someday.
response: He doesn’t say anything, and Father Osei lets him not say it. He has sat up with a great many people at this hour of a thing. The clock on the bookshelf goes. Out in the hall somebody sets a stack of hymnals down. Jack’s hand lets go of the hem of the Carhartt.

“I was going to marry her,” he says finally. “Someday. Not soon. I had a chair for her at our kitchen table on Glenwood, by the radiator, in my grandmother’s corner. And my grandmother sent word, at one in the morning, back in January: Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife.” He says it flat, a part number read off an invoice, because that’s the only way it’ll come out.

s21a.slug: SATURDAY · 4:25 PM · FATHER OSEI’S OFFICE — THE SAME DIRECTION
body: Father Osei is quiet a long time. His hand has come to rest on his left knee, the bad one. He takes his reading glasses off by the cord and holds them, and puts them on again.
“And so,” he says.

“And so why.” Jack tries. He opens his mouth to say why, why it’s her and not — why it has to be this, if he loves Skye — and nothing in him will line up. He has been trying to say it to himself since the levee. He has had two thousand miles.

What he gets to instead is his mother’s kitchen. Over the phone on the wall on Glenwood Avenue there’s a cross-stitch in a dime-store frame, blue thread on cream, a wedding present to his parents from one of Ma’s aunts, and he grew up reading it while he waited for the phone to ring, which in that house was a lot of waiting. He can see the stitches. He says it as it hangs, stitch for stitch:
“*Love does not consist in gazing at each other, but in looking outward together in the same direction.*” He looks at the floor. “Saint-Exupéry. It’s over the phone in my mother’s kitchen.”
Osei waits.

“Skye looks at me,” Jack says. “Father, she looks at me. Nobody ever — she’s the best thing that ever looked at me. She went to Mass to find out what I was doing in there. She knelt. She walked at the March in January, in the cold. She did all that to see me.” His hands are open on his knees and he doesn’t know when that happened. “And Lena looks where I’m looking. That’s all. That’s all it is. She’s looking at the same thing I’m looking at, she always has been, since the first week, and I turn around and she’s there.” He stops. “It doesn’t make Skye less. It makes it worse.”

“Your Frenchman was a pilot,” Osei says, after a while. “He came down in the Sahara once and walked for days with his mechanic before a Bedouin on a camel found them.” He turns the glasses over by their cord. “By the third day he did not have a theory. He had a mechanic, and his feet.”

body.text: “A man told me Monday not to wait on anybody,” Jack says. “I told him I was done waiting. Now I’m waiting three days.”
Osei’s eyebrows go up over the glasses. “Waiting is not the same as waiting *on*.”

body: “In January,” Jack says, “you asked me. To what question.” He hears his own voice in the little room, and it’s slower than it was ten minutes ago, the sentences coming one at a time and in order. “I think the question was which way I’m facing. I don’t know if that’s right. It’s the one I’ve got.”
Osei gives no verdict on it. “Then you have one more question than you had in January,” he says. “That is progress.”

body.text: “On the morning you left,” he says, “I told you the part of you that wished she had not stopped was not sorrow yet — to bring it to me when you could name it.”
“On the morning you left, you told me you were sorry you put it on her,” he says. “You are carrying something else now.”
“You promised me,” he says. “Not till you were back. You are back.”
“The last time you sat with me you could not name what you were carrying,” he says. “Try now.”

body: It isn’t that wish anymore. That one’s gone; he left it on a levee. He looks for what’s there now and finds it, and it’s smaller than he thought, and worse. “That it could’ve been both,” he says. “That I didn’t have to hurt her to tell the truth. That there was some way to do this where she doesn’t find out on her own porch with dinner on the stove.”
“That has a name,” says Father Osei. “It is grief. Grief is not a sin. I cannot absolve it.” He looks at the crucifix. “You carry it — and He carries it with you.”

body.text: And then, gently: “I put water in her hair at a quarter to five in the morning. She shut her eyes. I remember that.” He lets it sit. “She was a person, and you loved her as one.”
body.else: And then, gently: “I met her once, at the van, in the dark. I remember that she came.” He lets it sit. “She was a person, and you loved her as one.”

body: Jack nods at the floor. His eyes are wet, and Osei doesn’t look over.
Father Osei shifts in his chair and looks at his watch, and something comes into his face that Jack has seen across a chessboard.
“Jack,” he says. “You have been in that chair twenty minutes, and you have not confessed one thing.”
He laughs, small, from somewhere low in his belly. And Jack, who would not have bet a dollar there was a laugh in him this week, laughs too, one short helpless sound into the quiet office.

“No,” he says. “No, I — okay.” He sits up. He makes himself do it as Ma taught him, the examination, the small things, honestly, because he looks at the fortnight and nothing in it weighs. “Ash Wednesday, at one in the morning, Lena’s Nonc Clovis poured me bourbon on the porch, and I drank it so I wouldn’t want a cigarette. An hour into Lent. I wasn’t drunk. I wanted to be a little.”
Osei nods at the crucifix.
“Thursday morning I snapped at my roommate. For nothing. He was telling me about a coconut.”

body.text: “I said sorry. It was still mine.”
“I didn’t say sorry to him. I said it to a coconut.”
“I never said sorry. I wrote instead.”

body: “I’m fasting Fridays. Bread and water. Partly for God.” He makes himself finish it. “Partly to beat her at it.”

body.text: “I said it out loud in the van so she’d hear it.”
body.else: “I didn’t tell anybody. I still wanted her to find out.”

body: “Fasting out of pride is still fasting,” says Father Osei. “The pride you can leave with me.”

“And the guy she’s seeing. The one she’s ending it with tomorrow.” This one is harder, and he goes slower. “Everybody says he’s a good man, and he is, I think. And somewhere around Arizona I caught myself hoping he’d be a jerk about it. Tomorrow. So I could quit thinking he’s better than me.”
Osei’s hand turns over on his knee, palm up, and lies there. “Is there more?”
There’s one more.

choices.text: “And I bought a pack of cigarettes. I haven’t opened it.”
response: “And I bought a pack of cigarettes,” he says. “In El Paso. I haven’t opened it.”
“That is not a sin,” says Father Osei. “That is a very expensive rosary.” And, mildly: “Keep it in the pocket and keep the hand off it, and if the hand wins one day, come back.”

choices.text: “And on Mardi Gras I let her stay inside my coat. I wanted her there.”
response: “And on Mardi Gras I let her stay inside my coat,” he says. “At Rex, and on the levee that night for two hours — before we stopped, and after. It was cold. That’s not why. I wanted her there.”

Osei takes that in a moment. “To want is not to consent,” he says. “To be tempted is not to sin. You stopped. If there was a fault, it was standing so long where the wanting had no wall — a small imprudence, and you have told it, and it is told.” He looks at the crucifix. “What you do about Tuesday you have already said is yours. God does not usually waste a trip.”

choices.text: “And I told a thirteen-year-old ‘soon’ like I was promising to clean the gutters.”
response: “And I told a thirteen-year-old ‘soon,’” he says, “like I was promising to clean the gutters. Holding his ladder, in front of his sister. And Wednesday he asked me was it soon yet, and I said ‘Tuesday,’ and he believed me.”

This time Osei laughs out loud, his head back, his hand on the bad knee, and Jack sits there red to the ears with the corners of his own mouth gone. “That one,” Osei says, when he can, wiping his eye with the side of his finger, “I will absolve twice.”

choices.text: “And I told a thirteen-year-old ‘Tuesday’ like it was an answer.”
response: “And I told a thirteen-year-old ‘Tuesday,’” he says, “like it was an answer. On the curb, with his book bag on. He nodded like we’d shaken on something. He doesn’t know what Tuesday is.”

This time Osei laughs out loud, his head back, his hand on the bad knee, and Jack sits there red to the ears with the corners of his own mouth gone. “That one,” Osei says, when he can, wiping his eye with the side of his finger, “I will absolve twice.”

s21b.slug: SATURDAY · 4:45 PM · FATHER OSEI’S OFFICE — ƐYƐ
body: “You know you were not required to bring me any of that,” Father Osei says. “The Church asks you for the mortal sins, and you have brought me none. But she is glad when you bring the small ones. A doctor likes to see the healthy patient too, and a small cut bleeds a long time when nobody looks at it.” He turns his head and looks at Jack for the first time since they sat down. “And it lets Him heal what you would have called nothing.”
“For your penance,” says Father Osei. “On Tuesday, before you go to her door, say an Our Father for her. Slowly.” He waits until Jack looks up. “For her. Not for you.”

body.text: “I offered Lent for her,” Jack says. “On Wednesday.”
“Then Tuesday’s Our Father is a bead on the same string.”

body: Jack says the Act of Contrition from memory, Ma’s, the one she taught him at the kitchen table on Glenwood with her hand on the table beside his so he wouldn’t rush it. *O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended Thee, and I detest all my sins because of Thy just punishments, but most of all because they offend Thee, my God, who art all good and deserving of all my love.* He doesn’t rush it. He gets to *the near occasion of sin* and stops, because that’s the end of it.
Father Osei raises his right hand over him. No screen, no box; the late light in the office window behind them both and the crucifix in front.

“God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
Father Osei lets his hand down. Something in Jack’s shoulders that has been up around his ears since Fort Stockton comes down. He doesn’t do anything to make it.
He takes the stole off and kisses it and folds it over his arm, and sits back. “Did you eat today?”
“Gloria made me.”

“Then she has done my job.” He gets up, one hand on the arm of the chair for the knee. “Go and sleep. A man should not tell the truth on four hours’ sleep; it comes out crooked.” At the door he stops with his hand on the frame. “Ɛyɛ,” he says. “It is well.”

He hangs the purple stole on the hook for the vigil — the five o’clock is his — and goes to vest, and on his way past the turntable he sets the needle back down on the record, and the two guitars pick up where they left off, chasing each other round, as Jack goes out. The sacristy hall smells of candle wax and floor polish. Up in the tower the bell starts for the vigil.

s22.slug: SATURDAY · 5:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE FRONT STEPS
body: The first Saturday evening of Lent comes down gold over the courtyard, where the sprinkler is still in pieces on a tarp by the fountain with a pipe wrench lying across it. Behind him, through the doors, the organ starts and the people inside stand up and sing the opening hymn, “Lord, Who Throughout These Forty Days,” and it comes through the doors thin and steady.

A family comes up the steps past him late, a father carrying a little boy asleep on his shoulder with one shoe off, the mother behind with the shoe, and they go in, and the hymn comes out the door with them for a moment and is shut back in. The sun is low behind the bell tower. The cold that comes up the hill at this hour hasn’t got here yet.

He sits down on the top step. His hands are on his knees, doing nothing, and they don’t want anything to do. He takes the pack out and turns it over and looks at it, the red, the white, the seal, and puts it back in the breast pocket and does up the button.
Tomorrow is Sunday. It isn’t his.
The RAZR goes. SKYE (MISFIT), before her call time.

s22a.slug: SATURDAY · 5:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE FRONT STEPS
body: He shuts the phone and puts it back in the breast pocket, next to the pack.
Inside, the hymn ends, and there’s the sound of a church sitting down. At the bottom of the hill the Channel has gone to copper.
He gets up and goes in at the back as the first reading begins, and stands where he stood last night, by the holy water, with the lit church in front of him.
Three days.
